BPC-157 is a lab-made peptide that may help tendons, ligaments, muscles, and bones heal faster.

Researchers think it may help by lowering **inflammation** and helping new blood vessels grow in injured tissue.

BPC-157 is not **FDA-approved** , human research is still limited, and it is banned in competitive sport.

BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound-157) is a synthetic pentadecapeptide derived from a protective protein found in human gastric juice, investigated primarily for its regenerative and tissue-healing properties. Animal model research suggests it may accelerate recovery from tendon, ligament, muscle, and bone injuries while reducing **inflammation** and promoting **angiogenesis**.

The body of BPC-157 research consists primarily of **preclinical** animal studies, with very limited human clinical data. A 2025 **systematic review** identified 36 studies from 1993 to 2024, including 35 **preclinical** studies and only 1 clinical study.

Tendon Healing: Multiple rat studies demonstrated that BPC-157 improved structural, functional, and biomechanical outcomes following transection of the Achilles and quadriceps tendons. Treated animals showed improved load-to-failure, reduced inflammatory infiltrates, and enhanced tendon-to-bone healing.

Muscle Injury: In rat muscle transection and crush injury models, BPC-157 treatment improved muscle structure, function, and biomechanics, including improved load to failure, motor function indices, and reduced atrophy.

Ligament Repair: A rat medial collateral ligament (MCL) transection study found that BPC-157 reduced post-injury valgus instability and contracture while restoring biomechanical properties and motor function.

Bone Healing: In rabbit nonunion models, **intramuscular** BPC-157 performed comparably to autologous bone marrow or bone grafting in improving callus mineralization and bone defect resolution.

Human Data: Only one registered **clinical trial** (Phase I) exists, with unknown status since 2016. The only retrospective human study included 12 patients who received intra-articular BPC-157 for chronic knee pain, of whom 7 reported symptom improvement lasting more than 6 months.

BPC-157 occupies a complex regulatory gray area. In 2023, the FDA designated BPC-157 as a Category 2 bulk drug substance, meaning it cannot be compounded by commercial pharmaceutical companies, and there is insufficient evidence regarding potential harm to humans.

Not **FDA-approved** for any medical indication

Cannot legally be sold as a drug, food, or dietary supplement for human consumption

Legally sold as a "research chemical," not intended for human use

Not a DEA-scheduled substance, so possession is not illegal (unlike anabolic steroids)

Many medical clinics offer BPC-157 treatments despite lack of approval

The FDA has expressed safety concerns due to the lack of human **clinical trial** data and the potential for adverse effects from unregulated manufacturing.

BPC-157 represents one of the most intriguing regenerative peptides currently under investigation. **Preclinical** evidence consistently demonstrates its potential to accelerate healing across multiple tissue types through mechanisms involving **angiogenesis**, **growth factor** modulation, and **anti-inflammatory** effects. The peptide's favorable safety profile in animal studies and its stability across various administration routes have contributed to its growing popularity.

However, the critical limitation remains the near-complete absence of human **clinical trial** data. While animal studies are promising, they do not guarantee equivalent effects or safety in humans. Those considering BPC-157 should understand they are using an experimental compound with unknown long-term effects, sourced from an unregulated market where product quality and purity cannot be guaranteed.

For competitive athletes, BPC-157 use carries significant consequences due to its prohibited status across virtually all major sports organizations. For others, the decision to use BPC-157 should involve careful consideration of the limited evidence base, potential risks from unregulated products, and consultation with knowledgeable healthcare providers.

CJC-1295 is a synthetic **growth hormone**-releasing hormone (GHRH) analog that stimulates the pituitary gland to produce and release growth hormone (GH) and **insulin**-like **growth factor** 1 (**IGF-1**). Clinical research demonstrated that single injections increase GH levels 2- to 10-fold for six or more days and elevate **IGF-1** levels 1.5- to 3-fold for 9–11 days.

Enhanced fat **metabolism** and body composition

Improved recovery from exercise and injury

Potential anti-aging effects through **elevated** **IGF-1** levels

Increased collagen synthesis and skin elasticity

CJC-1295 without DAC produces a more pulsatile pattern of GH release, which some researchers believe better mimics natural physiology. The body normally releases GH in pulses, with the largest occurrence during deep sleep. CJC-1295 with DAC creates more sustained elevation of GH and **IGF-1** levels, which may benefit certain therapeutic applications but potentially blunts the natural pulsatile rhythm.

Beyond direct GH stimulation, CJC-1295 activates the broader GH/**IGF-1** axis. **Elevated** GH stimulates the liver to produce **IGF-1**, which mediates many of **growth hormone**'s anabolic effects on muscle, bone, and other tissues. Clinical trials showed **IGF-1** levels remained **elevated** above baseline for up to 28 days following multiple doses.

Weeks 1–2: Most users report improved sleep quality and more vivid dreams. Some experience mild water retention and increased appetite.

Weeks 2–4: Enhanced recovery from workouts becomes noticeable. Some users report improved skin quality and minor fat loss.

Weeks 4–8: More significant changes in body composition typically emerge, including increased muscle fullness and continued fat reduction. Strength gains may become apparent.

Weeks 8–12: Cumulative effects peak, with users often reporting the most dramatic improvements in lean mass, recovery, and overall body composition. Clinical research supports this timeline, showing **IGF-1** levels remained **elevated** above baseline for up to 28 days with repeated dosing, suggesting cumulative benefits.

The most significant clinical study on CJC-1295 was published in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & **Metabolism** in 2006. This **randomized**, **placebo-controlled**, **double-blind** trial examined pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and safety in healthy adults aged 21–61.

Single injections produced dose-dependent increases in GH concentrations of 2- to 10-fold lasting 6 or more days

**IGF-1** levels increased 1.5- to 3-fold for 9–11 days after a single dose

Multiple doses produced cumulative effects, with **IGF-1** remaining **elevated** above baseline for up to 28 days

No serious adverse reactions were reported

The peptide was safe and relatively well tolerated, particularly at doses of 30 or 60 μg/kg

Animal Research: A study published in the American Journal of Physiology demonstrated that once-daily administration of CJC-1295 normalized growth in GH-deficient models, supporting its potential therapeutic applications.

Additional Study (2009): Research published in **Growth Hormone** & IGF Research further confirmed the activation of the GH/**IGF-1** axis by CJC-1295, establishing its efficacy as a long-acting GHRH analog.

Important Note: A Phase II **clinical trial** investigating CJC-1295 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy was halted in 2006 following a patient death, though the relationship to the study drug was not definitively established.

CJC-1295 is not **FDA-approved** for human use. It exists in a regulatory gray area . It can be legally purchased for research purposes only but is not approved for human consumption or medical treatment.

In December 2024, the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee discussed CJC-1295 among other peptides, with the agency expressing concerns about cardiac risks and the potential for peptide impurities in compounded preparations. The FDA has moved to restrict compounding pharmacies from producing certain peptides, including CJC-1295, citing safety concerns and lack of adequate clinical data.

DAC technology represents a significant pharmacological advancement. After **subcutaneous** **injection**, CJC-1295 with DAC forms a covalent bond with circulating albumin through a reactive maleimido group, protecting the peptide from enzymatic degradation and renal **clearance**. sections.subheader: BDNF Upregulation and TrkB Receptor Activation
sections.body: Adamax is structurally derived from **Semax**, a heptapeptide analog of the ACTH(4-10) fragment. Its primary mechanism of interest involves the modulation of **brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)** expression and activation of its primary receptor, **TrkB**. In rodent hippocampal models, Semax administration at 50 μg/kg produced a 1.4-fold increase in BDNF protein levels and a 1.6-fold increase in TrkB tyrosine phosphorylation. Adamax is investigated within this same experimental framework to assess whether the **adamantyl modification** prolongs or enhances these interactions through greater enzymatic stability.

sections.subheader: Adamantyl Modification and Blood-Brain Barrier Penetration
sections.body: The defining structural feature of Adamax relative to standard Semax is the **adamantyl group** at the C-terminus, derived from Peptide P21. Adamantane is a lipophilic, cage-like hydrocarbon structure that is hypothesized to enhance **blood-brain barrier** penetration by increasing lipophilicity and reducing polar surface area. The N-terminal **acetyl group** provides complementary protection against aminopeptidase enzymatic degradation, extending the in vivo half-life relative to unmodified Semax. Together these two modifications are the focus of Adamax preclinical research — they are not properties confirmed in human trials.

Semax-derived peptides engage downstream intracellular cascades following **TrkB receptor** activation. In cell-based experimental systems, **MAPK/ERK** and **PI3K/Akt** signaling pathways are engaged — both associated with neuronal survival, protein synthesis, and synaptic remodeling. Additionally, the HGF/c-Met pathway has been implicated in Adamax-class compound research in the context of synaptogenesis and dendritic spine formation in APP/PS1 transgenic mouse models. These findings are preclinical and not consistent across all model systems.

Direct clinical data on Adamax does not exist — all human inference is extrapolated from the parent **Semax** compound. Semax was shown to bind specifically to membrane-associated sites in rat basal forebrain with a dissociation constant of 2.4 ± 1.0 nM. A single intranasal application at 50 μg/kg produced rapid increases in **BDNF** protein levels in the basal forebrain, alongside ~3-fold increases in exon III **BDNF mRNA** and ~2-fold increases in TrkB mRNA. Treated animals showed increased conditioned avoidance reactions. Adamax is studied within this framework to assess how the **adamantyl modification** alters these neurotrophin interactions. [Dolotov et al., 2006]

Adamax has no FDA-approved indication and is not approved for human use. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound. Notably, Adamax has been intercepted at the border as an unapproved designer peptide in New Zealand. In June 2025, New Zealand's Medicines Classification Committee received a submission recommending Adamax be classified as a **prescription medicine**. Researchers and users should verify the legal status in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use. It is not listed on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, but competitive athletes should verify via GlobalDRO.com before any research use.

All mechanistic data for Adamax is derived from **preclinical** animal studies, primarily on the parent Semax compound rather than Adamax itself. No **randomized controlled trial**, **phase 1 clinical trial**, or published human pharmacokinetic data exists for Adamax as of mid-2026. The adamantane modification's actual effect on **blood-brain barrier** penetration in humans remains unconfirmed. The compound's effects, safety profile, and long-term consequences in humans are entirely unknown. This is educational information, not medical advice.

A common research pairing for cognitive and anxiolytic effects. **Semax**-class compounds (including Adamax) target BDNF/TrkB upregulation and cognitive enhancement, while **Selank** (a tuftsin analog) has been associated with anxiolytic effects and modulation of GABAergic and serotonergic systems. The two compounds operate through distinct mechanisms, and their combination is used in nootropic research to target both cognitive performance and stress-response systems simultaneously. No formal **clinical trial** data exists for this combination.

Some researchers combine Adamax with standard Semax to compare the effect of the **adamantyl modification** directly. This pairing functions more as a research construct than a practical protocol, as both target identical upstream systems (BDNF/TrkB) through closely related mechanisms. There is no documented **synergistic** benefit to combining them, and dosing math becomes complex. For practical cognitive support protocols, one or the other is typically selected based on the desired stability and **blood-brain barrier** penetration profile.

No established clinical dosing protocol exists for Adamax. Extrapolating from **Semax** research, doses of 300–600 mcg once or twice daily via **intranasal** or **subcutaneous** administration are the most commonly reported research parameters. Intranasal delivery is the traditional route for Semax-class analogs due to proximity to the olfactory bulb and direct CNS access, though **subcutaneous injection** is also used in research settings. All dosing information is extrapolated from preclinical research on Semax analogs — no formal human dose-finding study has been conducted for Adamax.

Adamax ships as a lyophilized powder. A common starting point is a **10 mg vial** reconstituted with **2 mL bacteriostatic water**, yielding 5,000 mcg/mL. A 500 mcg dose equals 0.1 mL (10 units on an insulin syringe). Add the water slowly down the vial wall, swirl gently (do not shake), and allow full dissolution. Reconstituted peptide should be refrigerated at 4°C and used within 7 days. Lyophilized powder is stable for ≥24 months when stored at −20°C protected from light and moisture.

No formal human **safety** or tolerability data exists for Adamax. Theoretical concerns center on the **adamantyl modification** — a lipophilic adamantane group specifically investigated for enhanced **blood-brain barrier** penetration, meaning uncontrolled exposure carries uncharacterized risks of CNS delivery. Reported effects extrapolated from Semax-class compounds include transient headache, nasal irritation (intranasal route), light-headedness, and mild stimulatory effects. Active **psychiatric conditions**, pregnancy, and known CNS disorders are considered **contraindications** without physician oversight.

Lyophilized Adamax powder presents an **inhalation hazard** during weighing and reconstitution. All handling should be performed in a certified fume hood or biosafety cabinet with N95 respiratory protection, nitrile gloves, lab coat, and safety eyewear. Direct skin and eye contact must be avoided. Because the adamantane group is investigated for enhanced BBB penetration, any accidental mucosal or dermal exposure should be treated as a potential pharmacological event and managed per institutional protocols.

No formal pharmacokinetic study has been published for Adamax in humans or animals. Estimated **half-life** is approximately 2–4 hours based on Semax analog data, though the **N-terminal acetyl group** and **adamantyl modification** are specifically designed to extend enzymatic stability relative to native Semax. The acetyl group protects against aminopeptidase degradation; the adamantane group is hypothesized to reduce renal clearance through its lipophilic cage structure. These are mechanistic hypotheses, not confirmed human PK data.

Adamax is administered by **intranasal** spray or **subcutaneous** injection in research settings. The **intranasal** route is preferred for Semax-class analogs because it bypasses the blood-brain barrier via the olfactory epithelium and trigeminal nerve pathways, delivering compound directly to CNS tissue. However, the adamantane modification's enhanced **blood-brain barrier** penetration profile may make systemic **subcutaneous** dosing equally viable in preclinical models. Absorption kinetics, bioavailability, and Tmax values have not been formally published for Adamax as a standalone compound.

sections.body: MK-677 (Ibutamoren) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable **agonist** at the ghrelin **receptor** (GHSR-1a) — the same **receptor** targeted by injectable GHRPs like Ipamorelin and GHRP-6. Unlike those peptides, MK-677 is not a peptide at all; it is a synthetic spiroindoline-based compound designed specifically to survive oral administration and first-pass **metabolism** intact. Binding GHSR-1a on pituitary somatotrophs triggers **growth hormone** release through the same downstream calcium-signaling cascade as endogenous ghrelin, while also acting centrally in the hypothalamus.
sections.caption: MECHANISM OF ACTION

sections.body: Where injectable secretagogues produce a single, discrete GH pulse per dose, MK-677's long **half-life** (~24 hours) means a single oral dose keeps the ghrelin **receptor** engaged continuously, producing a sustained elevation in both the amplitude and number of natural GH pulses across the full 24-hour cycle rather than one isolated spike. This distinguishes its **pharmacokinetics** from short-acting GHRPs and is the basis for once-daily oral dosing.

**Growth hormone** released via GHSR-1a activation drives hepatic **IGF-1** production, the standard biomarker used to confirm response. Because the ghrelin **receptor** also mediates appetite and gastric motility in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, MK-677 reliably increases hunger — a mechanistic side effect shared with ghrelin itself, and one of the clearest ways MK-677's action differs in practice from the more selective injectable secretagogues like Ipamorelin.

• MK-677 is one of the few growth hormone secretagogues with genuine randomized, placebo-controlled human trial data — including a 2-year study in healthy older adults, not just short pharmacokinetic studies.

• A single **oral** dose produces a sustained rise in **growth hormone** and **IGF-1** lasting roughly 24 hours, unlike the single discrete pulse produced by short-acting injectable GHRPs.

• The best-known long-term trial (Nass et al., 2008) found MK-677 increased fat-free mass in older adults but did **not** improve physical function or strength outcomes over 2 years — a distinction often lost in casual discussion of the compound.

• Appetite stimulation and mild fluid retention are the most consistently reported effects across trials, tracing directly back to MK-677's ghrelin-mimetic mechanism.

Murphy et al. (1998) demonstrated in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial that oral MK-677 reversed the negative nitrogen balance induced by a hypocaloric diet in healthy adults, with treated subjects maintaining nitrogen balance while placebo subjects did not. This was among the first human demonstrations that an orally active ghrelin mimetic could produce **growth hormone** and **IGF-1** elevations sufficient to counteract a catabolic state — the finding that anchored later interest in sarcopenia and cachexia research. [Murphy MG, et al., 1998]

The most substantial human dataset comes from Nass et al. (2008), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults over 60 given MK-677 daily for 2 years. Fat-free mass increased significantly versus placebo, and **IGF-1** levels rose into the young-adult reference range and stayed there for the full study duration. However, the trial found no significant improvement in measures of physical function, muscle strength, or insulin sensitivity — treated subjects also had a higher, though not statistically dangerous, incidence of increased fasting glucose and mild insulin resistance. This is the key nuance in MK-677's research record: body-composition changes reliably occur, but they have not translated into functional performance gains in controlled trials. [Nass R, et al., 2008]

Because natural **growth hormone** secretion peaks during slow-wave sleep, and MK-677 sustains GH elevation across the sleep window specifically, several smaller studies have examined its effect on sleep quality. Findings suggest modest increases in REM sleep duration and subjective sleep quality in some cohorts, though data is far less extensive than the body-composition literature and effect sizes are inconsistent across studies.

A common research pairing that combines MK-677's sustained, 24-hour ghrelin-**receptor** activation with a GHRH analog's direct stimulation of the pituitary's own GH-releasing pathway. The two act on distinct **receptor** systems (GHSR-1a vs GHRH-**receptor**), which is the typical rationale researchers cite for combining a secretagogue with a GHRH analog rather than stacking two secretagogues. No **clinical trial** has tested this specific combination directly; the rationale is mechanistic, extrapolated from each compound's individual **pharmacology**.

Because both compounds act at the same **receptor** (GHSR-1a), this pairing is mechanistically redundant rather than synergistic — MK-677 already keeps the **receptor** engaged around the clock, so adding a short-acting GHRP on top does not add a distinct pathway the way a GHRH analog does. Researchers who want an oral-only protocol sometimes use MK-677 alone rather than combining it with an injectable in the same GHSR-1a class.

sections.subheader: Research Protocol Doses Reported in Published Literature
sections.body:
Research Disclaimer: Doses reported below are from published clinical and preclinical research protocols. MK-677 is not approved for human use by the FDA or any regulatory agency. This information is provided for research reference only and does not constitute a dosing recommendation.

All doses above are reported from published research protocols. Refer to the cited studies in the Research section above for original source data.

MK-677's side-effect profile follows directly from its mechanism: because it activates the ghrelin **receptor** systemically and continuously (rather than in a brief pulse), the most consistently reported effects across trials are increased appetite, mild fluid retention/edema, and transient lower-extremity numbness or tingling in some subjects. These are considered mechanistic — the same **receptor** that drives GH release also drives hunger signaling in the hypothalamus.

Human data: Human exposure includes multiple randomized, placebo-controlled trials, notably a 2-year study in adults over 60 (Nass et al., 2008) — among the longest continuous human safety datasets of any GH secretagogue discussed in this library. That trial reported a modest increase in fasting glucose and insulin resistance markers in the treatment group relative to placebo, without crossing into diagnosed diabetes; glucose monitoring is the most consistently recommended precaution in the literature.

Regulatory status: Not approved for human use by the FDA or any regulatory agency for any indication; it remains an investigational compound sold as a research chemical. It has been evaluated in GH-deficiency, sarcopenia, and cachexia research programs without reaching approval.

Contraindications commonly cited in research protocols include active malignancy (GH/IGF-1 elevation is a theoretical concern in hormone-sensitive or GH-sensitive tumor growth), pregnancy, and uncontrolled diabetes given the observed effect on insulin sensitivity.

MK-677's defining pharmacokinetic feature is that it is orally bioavailable and long-acting — the property that separates it from every injectable secretagogue in this library.

• Oral **Tmax** is approximately 30 minutes to 2 hours, with a terminal **elimination** **half-life** of approximately 24 hours, dramatically longer than Ipamorelin's ~2 hours or GHRP-6's ~1 hour.

• Because of this long half-life, once-daily oral dosing maintains meaningfully elevated **growth hormone** and **IGF-1** levels across the full 24-hour period rather than producing one discrete pulse, and **IGF-1** in particular stays elevated between doses due to its own longer physiological half-life.

• No **injection** or reconstitution is required — MK-677 is dosed as an oral capsule or solution, which is the practical basis for its popularity as a lower-friction alternative to injectable GH secretagogues.

name: Liraglutide
subtitle: A once-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist — the class predecessor to semaglutide and tirzepatide, still widely prescribed under Victoza and Saxenda.
description: Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist with 97% sequence homology to human GLP-1, modified with a fatty-acid side chain for albumin binding and extended action. Unlike the once-weekly semaglutide and tirzepatide, liraglutide requires once-daily subcutaneous dosing, titrated slowly upward to limit gastrointestinal side effects. It's FDA-approved under two brand names: Victoza for type 2 diabetes and Saxenda for chronic weight management, each with its own titration schedule and maximum dose. As an older, well-characterized GLP-1, it has the longest real-world safety record of any compound in this class.
contraindications: personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma

quickFacts.value: Refrigerate at 2-8°C, protected from light. Do not freeze.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier S — official FDA approval, on-label for the indications it is bought for.
Strongest documented use case: type 2 diabetes (Victoza, 2010) and chronic weight management (Saxenda, 2014).
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
The first GLP-1 approved for obesity, and still the reference point newer agonists are measured against.

sections.body: Liraglutide activates **GLP-1 receptors** throughout the body, sharing 97% sequence homology with native human GLP-1. It enhances glucose-dependent **insulin** secretion, suppresses **glucagon** release, slows gastric emptying, and acts on hypothalamic satiety centers to reduce food intake. A C16 fatty-acid side chain attached via a glutamic-acid linker enables reversible **albumin binding**, protecting the peptide from DPP-4 degradation and extending its **half-life** to roughly 13 hours — far short of semaglutide's ~7 days, which is why liraglutide requires daily rather than weekly injections.

Liraglutide is sold under two FDA-approved brand names targeting different indications: **Victoza** (0.6–1.8mg daily) for type 2 diabetes glycemic control, and **Saxenda** (titrated up to 3.0mg daily) for chronic weight management in patients with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related comorbidity. The molecule is identical; only the approved indication, max dose, and packaging differ.

Liraglutide has the longest clinical track record of any **GLP-1 receptor agonist**, with over a decade of post-marketing safety data since Victoza's 2010 approval. The LEAD trial program established its glycemic efficacy in type 2 diabetes; the SCALE program established weight-loss efficacy (Saxenda, approved 2014), with average placebo-subtracted weight loss around 5–6% — modest compared to semaglutide or tirzepatide, reflecting its shorter **half-life** and lower peak systemic exposure.

Liraglutide is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved** under both Victoza (type 2 diabetes) and Saxenda (chronic weight management) indications. It is a legitimate pharmaceutical, not a research chemical — it should only be obtained through a licensed prescriber and pharmacy. Off-label or self-directed use outside a prescribing relationship carries the same legal and safety concerns as any prescription-only medication.

Liraglutide is typically used as a standalone metabolic agent rather than stacked with growth or healing peptides. Clinicians occasionally combine it with resistance training and a higher-protein diet to offset lean-mass loss during a weight-loss course, but there is no established peptide-stacking protocol — unlike newer GLP-1s, it is rarely paired with GH secretagogues in research/clinic settings, largely because most patients on liraglutide are managed through standard endocrinology rather than peptide clinics.

Both Victoza and Saxenda start at **0.6mg once daily** subcutaneously for one week, then increase in 0.6mg increments at weekly-to-monthly intervals to limit nausea and GI upset. Victoza's typical maintenance dose is 1.2–1.8mg daily; Saxenda titrates further to a 3.0mg daily maintenance dose for weight management. Unlike semaglutide or tirzepatide, there is no weekly-injection version — liraglutide requires **daily** dosing for the life of the therapy, delivered via a pre-filled pen.

The most common side effects are gastrointestinal: **nausea**, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation, typically worst during dose titration. Boxed warning: risk of **medullary thyroid carcinoma** observed in rodent studies, which is why personal/family history of MTC or MEN 2 is an absolute contraindication. Other risks include **pancreatitis**, gallbladder disease, and (rarely) acute kidney injury secondary to dehydration from GI side effects. Pregnancy is contraindicated.

Subcutaneous **bioavailability** is approximately 55%, with peak plasma concentration reached 8–12 hours after dosing. The fatty-acid **albumin-binding** mechanism slows both absorption and clearance, giving liraglutide its ~13-hour half-life — long enough for once-daily dosing but far shorter than the fatty-diacid modification used in semaglutide, which extends half-life to about 7 days. Steady state is reached within 4–5 days of consistent daily dosing.

name: Exenatide
subtitle: The first-in-class GLP-1 receptor agonist, derived from a peptide found in Gila monster saliva — sold as Byetta and Bydureon.
description: Exenatide is a synthetic version of exendin-4, a peptide originally isolated from the saliva of the Gila monster. It shares only 53% sequence homology with human GLP-1 — far less than semaglutide or liraglutide — which is precisely why it naturally resists DPP-4 enzymatic degradation without needing a fatty-acid modification. It was the first GLP-1 receptor agonist to reach market (Byetta, 2005), dosed twice daily before meals, followed by an extended-release once-weekly formulation (Bydureon, 2012). It remains FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes glycemic control.
contraindications: personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma

quickFacts.value: Refrigerate at 2-8°C, protected from light. Do not freeze.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier S — official FDA approval, the first GLP-1 receptor agonist to market.
Strongest documented use case: glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes (Byetta, 2005; Bydureon, 2012).
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Weight loss is a documented secondary effect, not an approved indication.

sections.body: Exenatide is a synthetic analog of **exendin-4**, a peptide first isolated from the venomous saliva of the Gila monster (*Heloderma suspectum*). It shares only 53% sequence homology with human **GLP-1** — far less than semaglutide or liraglutide — and this divergence is exactly what makes it naturally resistant to **DPP-4** enzymatic degradation, without requiring the fatty-acid modifications used in later-generation GLP-1s.

Like other **GLP-1 receptor agonists**, exenatide enhances glucose-dependent **insulin** secretion, suppresses inappropriate **glucagon** release, slows gastric emptying, and promotes satiety. It was the first compound in this class to reach market, establishing the therapeutic template that semaglutide, tirzepatide, and dulaglutide later built on.

Approved in 2005 as **Byetta**, exenatide was the first GLP-1 receptor agonist available to patients, predating semaglutide by over a decade. The extended-release microsphere formulation, **Bydureon**, was approved in 2012, reformulating the same molecule into a once-weekly depot injection. Because it's been in clinical use the longest of any GLP-1, it has an extensive long-term safety record.

Exenatide is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved** for type 2 diabetes under both the Byetta and Bydureon brand names. It is a legitimate pharmaceutical and should only be obtained through a licensed prescriber and pharmacy.

Exenatide is prescribed as a standalone diabetes therapy, often alongside metformin or other oral glycemic agents rather than other injectable peptides. It is not typically part of a peptide-clinic stacking protocol.

**Byetta** is dosed at 5mcg subcutaneously twice daily, within 60 minutes before the two largest meals of the day, increasing to 10mcg BID after one month if tolerated. **Bydureon** (extended-release microspheres) is dosed at a fixed 2mg once weekly, any time of day, without regard to meals — the two formulations are not interchangeable on a mcg-for-mcg basis.

**Nausea** is the most common side effect, especially with Byetta's twice-daily dosing around meals. Other GI effects include vomiting and diarrhea. Serious risks include **pancreatitis**, and Bydureon carries the same rodent-derived **medullary thyroid carcinoma** boxed warning as other GLP-1s. Exenatide should be avoided in severe renal impairment, as it's cleared renally and doesn't have the albumin-binding protection some newer GLP-1s do.

Byetta reaches peak plasma concentration about 2 hours after injection with a **half-life** of roughly 2.4 hours — short enough to require twice-daily dosing. Bydureon uses biodegradable polymer microspheres that release exenatide slowly over weeks, producing a much flatter, sustained plasma profile that supports once-weekly dosing despite the underlying molecule's short native half-life.

name: Orforglipron
subtitle: The first oral, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist pill with no food or water restrictions — FDA-approved in 2026 as Foundayo.
description: Orforglipron is a fundamentally different kind of GLP-1 medicine: a small-molecule, non-peptide oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, taken as a once-daily tablet at any time of day, with or without food — unlike semaglutide's oral form (Rybelsus), which must be taken fasted with a small sip of water and a 30-minute food/drink delay. Developed by Eli Lilly under the development code LY3502970, orforglipron received FDA approval on April 1, 2026 under the brand name Foundayo, for adults with obesity or overweight with a weight-related medical problem. Its inclusion here alongside injectable peptides mirrors how MK-677 — also a non-peptide, orally active compound — sits in REGEN's catalog as a notable exception to the peptide-only norm.
contraindications: personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma

quickFacts.value: Non-peptide, oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist
Room temperature, sealed, away from light and moisture. No refrigeration or reconstitution required.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier S — official FDA approval as Foundayo, April 2026.
Strongest documented use case: weight reduction and glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
An oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist, so it avoids the peptide formulation constraints of injectables.

sections.body: Orforglipron is **not a peptide** — it's a small-molecule, non-peptide compound that activates the **GLP-1 receptor**, engineered to survive digestion intact and absorb through the gut without the specialized absorption-enhancer technology semaglutide's oral form (Rybelsus) requires. Structurally unrelated to native GLP-1 or exendin-4, it was designed from the ground up as an orally bioavailable small molecule rather than a modified peptide.

The defining practical advantage of orforglipron over Rybelsus (oral semaglutide) is dosing flexibility: it can be taken **any time of day, with or without food**, with no fasting requirement and no minimum water intake rule. This removes the biggest adherence barrier of the prior oral GLP-1 option, where a missed fasting window meant a missed effective dose.

Orforglipron, developed by **Eli Lilly** under development code **LY3502970**, received **FDA approval on April 1, 2026** under the brand name **Foundayo**, for adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related medical problem. It is the first oral GLP-1 pill approved with no food or water restrictions.

Orforglipron is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved** as of April 2026. It is a legitimate, approved pharmaceutical and should only be obtained through a licensed prescriber and pharmacy — not through unregulated research-chemical channels, regardless of how it may be marketed there.
As a newly approved oral medication, orforglipron is prescribed as a standalone weight-management therapy through standard medical channels, not as part of an informal peptide-stacking protocol.

Orforglipron is available in six tablet strengths — **0.8mg, 2.5mg, 5.5mg, 9mg, 14.5mg, and 17.2mg** — taken once daily, with the dose titrated upward gradually to limit gastrointestinal side effects, following the same general titrate-slowly principle used across the GLP-1 class.

As with other **GLP-1 receptor agonists**, the most common side effects are gastrointestinal — **nausea**, diarrhea, constipation, and vomiting — typically most pronounced during dose titration. The class boxed warning for **medullary thyroid carcinoma** risk (based on rodent data) applies. Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, and pregnancy are contraindications shared across the GLP-1 class.

Orforglipron is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract without requiring the specialized absorption-enhancer (SNAC) technology that oral semaglutide depends on, which is what allows it to be dosed without fasting. Its **half-life** of roughly 29–49 hours supports once-daily oral dosing with steady accumulation over the first 1–2 weeks of a given dose level.

name: NAD+
subtitle: A naturally occurring cellular coenzyme central to energy metabolism and DNA repair — sold as an IV, injectable, and oral longevity supplement.
description: NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a coenzyme found in every living cell, central to mitochondrial energy production and DNA-repair enzyme activity. Cellular NAD+ levels decline with age, which has driven a wave of consumer interest in supplementing it directly via IV infusion, injection, or oral precursors. Unlike a conventional drug, NAD+ doesn't behave with a simple circulating half-life — it's rapidly taken up and used intracellularly. It's sold over-the-counter as an oral dietary supplement, and administered by IV or injection at wellness clinics, but it is not an FDA-approved drug for any indication, and anti-aging claims made about it are not FDA-evaluated.

standardDose.frequency: varies by route — daily (SC/IM) to weekly (IV infusion)

reconstitution.notes: Injectable NAD+ protocols vary widely by vendor and clinic; a common convention is a 500mg vial reconstituted with 5mL bacteriostatic water. IV infusion is typically clinic-prepared and administered over 1–4 hours.

halfLife: Not a typical circulating half-life — rapidly taken up and metabolized intracellularly rather than persisting in plasma

quickFacts.value: Cellular coenzyme / dietary supplement (not a peptide)
No trademarked brand — sold as a generic coenzyme supplement
OTC dietary supplement (oral); injectable/IV forms are clinic-compounded and not FDA-approved as a drug
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier C — most supporting human data comes from precursors rather than from NAD+ itself.
Strongest documented use case: correcting measured NAD+ decline, largely inferred from NR and NMN trials.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Intravenous NAD+ specifically has little controlled human evidence behind it.

sections.body: **NAD+** is a coenzyme present in every living cell, acting as an electron carrier in mitochondrial ATP production and as a required substrate for **sirtuin** and **PARP** enzymes involved in DNA repair and cellular stress response. Because it is consumed continuously by these processes, cellular NAD+ pools decline measurably with age — the basis for interest in exogenous supplementation.

NAD+ is administered via IV infusion, subcutaneous or intramuscular injection, or oral capsule. Oral bioavailability of intact NAD+ is limited, which is part of why IV and injectable routes are popular at wellness clinics — they bypass first-pass gut metabolism, though direct comparative bioavailability data across routes in humans is limited.

Most human evidence on raising NAD+ levels comes from studies of oral **precursors** (NMN, NR) rather than direct NAD+ administration, and even that literature is still early — small trials, short durations, and mixed results on hard clinical endpoints. Claims around IV/injectable NAD+ for energy, cognition, or longevity are largely anecdotal and clinic-marketed rather than backed by controlled human trials.

Oral NAD+ is available **over-the-counter** as a dietary supplement in the US. Injectable and IV NAD+ are typically **compounded** and administered at wellness clinics; the FDA has scrutinized NAD+ in recent compounding rulemaking discussions. NAD+ is **not an FDA-approved drug** for any indication, and longevity/anti-aging claims made about it have not been FDA-evaluated. Verify local compounding-pharmacy regulations before pursuing injectable/IV administration.

NAD+ is frequently offered alongside **glutathione** and B-vitamin injections at wellness/longevity clinics as part of broader IV-therapy menus, positioned as complementary cellular-health support rather than a peptide-stacking protocol in the traditional sense.

Injectable/subcutaneous protocols commonly use **50–100mg** daily or a few times weekly. Clinic-administered IV infusions use much larger doses — **250–750mg** — delivered slowly over 1–4 hours, since rapid IV infusion of NAD+ is associated with infusion-related discomfort (flushing, chest tightness, cramping) at high infusion rates.

The most commonly reported side effects are **infusion-related** — flushing, mild chest or abdominal tightness, cramping, or nausea, especially when IV NAD+ is administered too quickly. These typically resolve by slowing the infusion rate. Injectable/subcutaneous forms can cause local injection-site irritation. Long-term safety data at the doses used in wellness clinics remains limited.

NAD+ does not behave like a typical small-molecule drug with a defined plasma **half-life** — it is rapidly taken up by cells and consumed by intracellular enzymatic processes rather than circulating and being cleared systemically. This is part of why direct human pharmacokinetic data for exogenous NAD+ is sparse compared to its precursor compounds.

name: Glutathione
subtitle: The body's master antioxidant tripeptide — sold as an IV/injectable and oral wellness supplement for detox, skin, and liver support.
description: Glutathione is a tripeptide (glutamate-cysteine-glycine) produced naturally in the liver and considered the body's primary intracellular antioxidant, neutralizing free radicals and supporting detoxification pathways. Though technically a tripeptide, it's marketed and used almost exclusively as a wellness supplement rather than a research peptide — sold as an oral/liposomal capsule and as an IV or intramuscular injectable at wellness clinics, often alongside NAD+ on the same infusion menu. It's regulated as a dietary/food ingredient rather than an approved drug, and injectable glutathione marketed specifically for skin lightening has drawn FDA scrutiny.

standardDose.frequency: varies by route — a few times weekly (IM/IV) to daily (oral)

reconstitution.notes: Injectable glutathione protocols vary by vendor; a common convention is a 600mg vial reconstituted with bacteriostatic water for IM/IV clinic administration.

halfLife: Very short in circulation (minutes) — rapidly recycled intracellularly via the glutathione redox cycle rather than persisting as free plasma glutathione

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a generic antioxidant supplement
OTC dietary supplement (oral); injectable skin-lightening use is not FDA-approved and has drawn FDA import warnings
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier D — no approval for the uses it is sold for, and the FDA has warned specifically about compounded injectable forms.
Strongest documented use case: endogenous antioxidant function; supplementation outcomes are poorly evidenced.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Oral bioavailability is low, which is why it is marketed by injection — the route carrying the warning.

sections.body: **Glutathione** is a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, synthesized primarily in the liver. Its central thiol (-SH) group allows it to neutralize reactive oxygen species and regenerate other antioxidants like vitamins C and E, making it a core component of the body's intracellular antioxidant defense and **detoxification** machinery, including conjugation reactions in liver Phase II metabolism.

Rather than being consumed and excreted like a typical supplement, glutathione is continuously **recycled** between its reduced (GSH) and oxidized (GSSG) forms via glutathione reductase, an enzymatic cycle that regenerates the antioxidant pool from within cells rather than relying solely on external replenishment.

Oral glutathione has historically faced **bioavailability** questions, since it's broken down by digestive enzymes before absorption — liposomal and S-acetyl formulations were developed to address this. Injectable/IV glutathione bypasses digestion entirely and is popular in wellness clinics for detox, skin, and liver-support claims, though robust controlled human trial data supporting these specific outcome claims is limited.

Glutathione is available **over-the-counter** as an oral dietary supplement — the FDA treats it as a GRAS (generally recognized as safe) food/dietary ingredient, not an approved drug. Injectable glutathione marketed specifically for **skin lightening** is **not FDA-approved** for that use, and the FDA has issued import alerts regarding unapproved injectable skin-lightening glutathione products sourced from overseas.
Glutathione is frequently paired with **NAD+** on wellness-clinic IV menus as complementary cellular-health/antioxidant support, rather than combined with peptides in a dosing-protocol sense.

Injectable protocols commonly use **200–600mg** IM or IV, a few times weekly, at wellness clinics. Oral liposomal supplements are commonly dosed at **250–1000mg** daily. There is no FDA-established clinical dosing standard for either route.

Glutathione is generally well tolerated. Rare reports include mild **abdominal cramping** or bloating with oral use, and injection-site irritation with IM/IV use. Nebulized or very high-dose IV glutathione has been associated with rare **bronchospasm** reports in patients with asthma. Sulfa/sulfite-sensitive individuals should discuss injectable formulations with a clinician, as some preparations contain sulfite preservatives.

Free circulating glutathione has a very short plasma **half-life** — on the order of minutes — because it's rapidly taken up and recycled intracellularly via the glutathione redox cycle rather than persisting in the bloodstream like a conventional drug.

name: Somatropin (HGH)
subtitle: Recombinant human growth hormone — a 191-amino-acid polypeptide identical to the body's own pituitary GH, sold under brands including Humatrope and Genotropin.
description: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone, a 191-amino-acid single-chain polypeptide identical in sequence to the growth hormone naturally produced by the pituitary gland. It's FDA-approved under multiple brand names for specific indications — pediatric growth failure, adult growth hormone deficiency, and, for certain brands, conditions like HIV-associated wasting or short bowel syndrome. Dosing is highly individualized and titrated by a prescriber based on IGF-1 lab levels, not self-directed. Distribution or possession of somatropin for unapproved uses such as bodybuilding or anti-aging is a specific federal crime in the US, reflecting its history of non-medical misuse.

reconstitution.notes: Common clinical convention: a 5–10mg lyophilized vial reconstituted with 1–2mL bacteriostatic water, dosed daily via subcutaneous injection. Exact vial size and dilution vary by brand and pen device.

halfLife: ~20–30 minutes in serum (biological effects last much longer, mediated downstream through IGF-1)

quickFacts.value: Humatrope, Genotropin, Norditropin, Omnitrope, Saizen, Nutropin, Serostim, Zomacton
Prescription-only, FDA-approved for specific indications. Distribution/possession for unapproved use is a federal crime under 21 U.S.C. § 333(e)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier S — official FDA approval, in continuous clinical use since 1985.
Strongest documented use case: growth hormone deficiency in children and adults.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Performance, physique and anti-ageing use is entirely off-label.

sections.body: Somatropin is manufactured via recombinant DNA technology to be structurally identical to the 191-amino-acid **growth hormone** naturally secreted by the pituitary gland. It binds **GH receptors** throughout the body, most importantly in the liver, stimulating production of **IGF-1** — the hormone that mediates most of GH's downstream growth, tissue-repair, and metabolic effects.

Beyond linear growth in children, somatropin promotes **lipolysis** (fat breakdown), supports lean-mass maintenance, and influences glucose metabolism — it has a mild insulin-antagonist effect at higher doses, which is part of why fasting glucose is monitored during therapy.

Somatropin brands are FDA-approved for a range of indications depending on the specific product: pediatric growth hormone deficiency and growth failure, adult growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, and — for specific brands — HIV-associated wasting (**Serostim**) or short bowel syndrome (**Zorbtive**). Each brand has its own FDA-approved label and indication set; they are not interchangeable off-label without a prescriber's guidance.

Somatropin is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved** for the specific indications listed on each brand's label. Distributing or possessing somatropin for unapproved uses — bodybuilding, anti-aging, athletic performance — is a **federal crime** in the US under **21 U.S.C. § 333(e)**, a statute specific to human growth hormone that goes beyond ordinary prescription-drug law, reflecting its history of non-medical misuse. It should only be obtained through a licensed prescriber for an approved indication.

In its approved medical context, somatropin is prescribed as a standalone hormone-replacement therapy managed by an endocrinologist, with regular IGF-1 and glucose monitoring — not combined with other peptides in a stacking protocol.

Dosing varies substantially by brand, age, and indication. As examples: **Genotropin/Omnitrope** pediatric dosing typically starts up to 0.04–0.08 mg/kg/week divided into daily doses; **adult GH-deficiency** dosing typically starts much lower, around 0.1–0.2mg/day, and is titrated upward by a prescriber based on **IGF-1** lab levels and tolerability. This is not a self-directed dose — it requires physician oversight and lab monitoring.

Common effects include injection-site reactions, **fluid retention**/edema, joint pain, and headache, especially early in therapy or at higher doses. More serious risks include worsened **insulin resistance**/elevated blood glucose, intracranial hypertension (rare), and theoretical concerns about tumor growth stimulation, which is why active malignancy is a contraindication. Diabetic retinopathy can worsen with GH therapy.

sections.subheader: Short Serum Half-Life, Longer Downstream Effect
sections.body: Somatropin's serum **half-life** is short — roughly 20–30 minutes — but its biological effects last far longer because they're mediated through **IGF-1**, which has a much longer half-life and sustains the downstream metabolic and tissue effects well after the GH itself has cleared.

name: KPV
subtitle: A synthetic tripeptide fragment of alpha-MSH studied for anti-inflammatory effects without the pigmentation or arousal effects of full melanocortin agonists.
description: KPV (Lysine-Proline-Valine) is a synthetic tripeptide corresponding to the C-terminal fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), residues 11-13. It retains α-MSH's anti-inflammatory melanocortin signaling but, being only three amino acids, lacks the pigmentation-darkening and sexual-arousal effects seen with full-length analogs like Melanotan II. Research interest centers on gut inflammation, skin inflammation, and wound healing via modulation of the NF-κB pathway. It's sold only as a research compound — no clinical trial or FDA approval data exists.

sources.title: PepT1-mediated tripeptide KPV uptake reduces intestinal inflammation

sections.subheader: α-MSH Fragment Without the Pigmentation Effects
sections.body: KPV is a synthetic tripeptide reproducing the C-terminal three residues (Lys-Pro-Val) of **alpha-MSH**, the parent hormone behind Melanotan II. Because it lacks the rest of the α-MSH sequence, KPV retains **melanocortin-pathway anti-inflammatory** signaling without triggering the skin-darkening or libido effects associated with full-length melanocortin agonists.

Preclinical research points to KPV suppressing **NF-κB** activation, a master transcription factor driving inflammatory cytokine production. This mechanism underlies most of its studied applications — gut inflammation (colitis models), skin inflammation, and general wound-healing support — though nearly all supporting data is preclinical or in-vitro rather than human clinical evidence.

KPV's anti-inflammatory and gut-protective effects have been studied primarily in **animal colitis models** and cell-based assays. No published human clinical trial exists. Its popularity as a research/self-experimentation compound has outpaced the formal evidence base considerably.

KPV has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO — research use only). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of KPV in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use — regulations on unapproved peptide research chemicals vary widely and change frequently.

A common research pairing targeting **gut health** — KPV's anti-inflammatory melanocortin signaling alongside **BPC-157**'s gastric and soft-tissue repair effects. This combination, along with GHK-Cu and TB-500, forms the basis of the popular KLOW blend.
KPV is also paired with **GHK-Cu** in skin-focused research protocols, combining KPV's anti-inflammatory effects with GHK-Cu's collagen-remodeling and wound-healing properties.

Vendor/research-typical protocols use **200–500mcg** subcutaneous once daily. Oral capsule and topical forms are also sold by some vendors, though no formal dose-finding study exists for any route — all figures here reflect informal research-community convention, not clinical validation.

No formal human safety or tolerability data exists for KPV. Given its origin as an α-MSH fragment, theoretical concerns include unknown effects on **appetite** or **mood** at higher doses, though KPV specifically lacks the receptor-binding profile responsible for Melanotan II's stronger appetite/libido effects. Active CNS or psychiatric conditions and pregnancy are treated as precautionary contraindications.

As an unmodified tripeptide with no stabilizing modifications, KPV is expected to have a very short **half-life** — likely on the order of minutes, consistent with other small unmodified peptides. No formal human pharmacokinetic study has been published to confirm this.

name: Epithalon
subtitle: A synthetic tetrapeptide analog of a natural pineal gland peptide, studied for telomerase activation and circadian regulation.
description: Epithalon (also spelled Epitalon) is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly (AEDG), designed as an analog of epithalamin, a naturally occurring pineal gland peptide. It has been studied — primarily by Russian researchers, notably Vladimir Khavinson's group — in small and preclinical studies for telomerase activation, pineal gland/melatonin regulation, and circadian rhythm effects. It's sold exclusively as a research compound; no FDA approval or large-scale human trial exists.

Strongest documented use case: pineal peptide bioregulation, studied mainly in Russian-language literature.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
The telomerase-activation claim is the reason it sells and the part with the least independent support.

sources.title: Overview of Epitalon — Highly Bioactive Pineal Tetrapeptide with Promising Properties

sections.body: Epithalon (**AEDG**: Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) is a synthetic tetrapeptide designed to mimic **epithalamin**, a naturally occurring pineal gland peptide extract. Research interest centers on the pineal gland's role in regulating **melatonin** production and, by extension, circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycling.

Epithalon is best known for preclinical research (Khavinson et al.) investigating **telomerase** activation — the enzyme that maintains telomere length at chromosome ends — in cell culture and animal models. This research forms the basis of its popularity in longevity circles, though direct human evidence for telomerase effects remains limited.

The bulk of epithalon's published research comes from a small number of research groups, primarily in Russia, using small sample sizes and older publication standards. Cell-culture and animal studies suggest effects on **telomerase activity** and circadian markers, but rigorous, independently replicated human randomized controlled trials are lacking.

Epithalon has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). No formal human pharmacokinetic or dose-finding study has been conducted. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of epithalon in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

Epithalon is sometimes paired with **DSIP** in sleep- and circadian-focused research protocols, combining epithalon's pineal/melatonin-pathway research angle with DSIP's studied delta-sleep-inducing effects. No formal trial data exists for this or any epithalon combination.

The most commonly cited research protocol uses **5–10mg daily** via subcutaneous injection for a **10–20 day course**, repeated a few times per year rather than used continuously. This cycling pattern comes from the original Khavinson-group research design, not from a formal human dose-finding trial.

No formal human safety or tolerability data exists for epithalon at scale. Given its studied interest in telomerase and cell-cycle-related pathways, active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication until more is understood about its effects in that context. Pregnancy is also a precautionary contraindication.

No study has directly measured epithalon's plasma **half-life** in humans. Based on the general pharmacokinetics of short, unmodified peptides — which typically show plasma half-lives of 2–15 minutes — epithalon's circulating half-life is expected to be on the order of minutes, though this is an extrapolation rather than a confirmed measurement.

name: DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide)
subtitle: A nonapeptide originally isolated from rabbit brain, studied for its role in inducing delta-wave (deep) sleep.
description: DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide) is a nonapeptide with the sequence Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu, first isolated from the brains of rabbits during studies of sleep physiology. It's studied for effects on delta-wave (deep, slow-wave) sleep induction, stress-response modulation, and circadian regulation. Its native human plasma half-life is extremely short — a matter of minutes — and no formal clinical dosing protocol has been established. It's sold only as a research compound.

reconstitution.notes: 5mg vial + 2mL bacteriostatic water = 2500mcg/mL.

contraindications: active psychiatric conditions without physician oversight

Not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier D — a handful of small human studies from the 1970s and 80s, then effectively abandoned.
Strongest documented use case: sleep-onset modulation, on evidence that never progressed past early trials.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Small double-blind trials in the 1980s-90s (Schneider-Helmert 1992, N=16) reported modest sleep improvements, but were never replicated at modern scale.

sources.title: Effects of Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide on Sleep of Chronic Insomniac Patients: A Double-Blind Study

sections.body: DSIP was first identified in the 1970s in studies where blood from **sleep-deprived** rabbits was found to induce delta-wave (deep, slow-wave) sleep patterns when transferred to other animals. The nonapeptide responsible was isolated and named accordingly. Its exact receptor mechanism in humans remains incompletely characterized compared to modern, well-mapped GPCR-targeting peptides.

Beyond its namesake sleep effect, DSIP has been studied for roles in **stress-response** buffering and circadian regulation, with some research suggesting interaction with the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Most of this evidence comes from older animal studies rather than modern, well-controlled human trials.

Much of the foundational DSIP research dates to the 1970s-1990s, predating modern clinical trial standards. Some small human studies explored effects on sleep architecture and stress hormones, but the evidence base is thin and outdated by current standards, with no large modern randomized controlled trial.

DSIP has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of DSIP in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

A common research pairing for sleep and circadian-rhythm research, combining DSIP's studied delta-sleep effects with **epithalon**'s pineal-gland/melatonin-pathway research angle. No formal trial data exists for this combination.

Vendor/research-typical dosing is **100–300mcg** subcutaneous, administered shortly before bed. No formal clinical dose-finding study exists for general research use — this range reflects informal research-community convention only.

No modern, comprehensive human safety data exists for DSIP. Older studies reported it as generally well tolerated at studied doses, but formal adverse-event surveillance at scale has never been conducted. Active psychiatric conditions and pregnancy are treated as precautionary contraindications.

DSIP has a documented human plasma **half-life** of approximately 7-8 minutes. In vitro stability is even shorter — about 15 minutes — due to a specific aminopeptidase-like enzyme that rapidly degrades it. This very short half-life is part of why it's dosed shortly before the sleep window it's intended to influence.

name: Kisspeptin-10
subtitle: A decapeptide fragment of human kisspeptin, sitting upstream of the entire reproductive hormone axis by triggering GnRH release.
description: Kisspeptin-10 is a synthetic decapeptide corresponding to the active C-terminal fragment of the human KISS1 gene product. It activates the KISS1R (GPR54) receptor on GnRH neurons, triggering pulsatile GnRH release and downstream LH/FSH secretion — placing it upstream of the entire hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. It's studied in reproductive endocrinology and fertility research, and more recently in libido and HPG-axis research contexts. No formal human dosing protocol or FDA approval exists; it's sold only as a research compound.

reconstitution.notes: 5mg vial + 2mL bacteriostatic water = 2500mcg/mL.

halfLife: Very short (minutes) — unmodified decapeptide with rapid enzymatic clearance

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a research compound
Not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier B — controlled human studies confined to reproductive endocrinology, with no approval.
Strongest documented use case: stimulating LH and downstream sex-hormone release in human physiology research.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Nearly all human data is mechanistic and short-duration — it establishes the axis, not an outcome.

sections.body: Kisspeptin-10 activates the **KISS1R** (GPR54) receptor on **GnRH**-producing neurons in the hypothalamus, triggering pulsatile GnRH release. This in turn drives **LH** and **FSH** secretion from the pituitary — placing kisspeptin signaling upstream of essentially the entire **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis**, making it a master regulatory node for reproductive hormone production.

Kisspeptin signaling was identified as essential for the onset of **puberty** and normal reproductive function — loss-of-function mutations in the KISS1R gene cause failure to enter puberty. This foundational biology is why kisspeptin-10 is studied in fertility and reproductive endocrinology research, including as a potential tool for triggering ovulation in IVF protocols.

Most published kisspeptin-10 research centers on its role in **LH/FSH** secretion, ovulation triggering, and puberty physiology, studied in controlled clinical research settings (e.g. IVF ovulation-trigger studies) rather than as a general-purpose self-administered compound. Libido and general HPG-axis research use is a newer, less-studied application.

Kisspeptin-10 has no FDA-approved indication for general use and is **not approved for human consumption** outside controlled clinical research settings. It is sold to the general public exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of kisspeptin-10 in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

Kisspeptin-10 is typically used as a standalone research compound targeting the **HPG axis** rather than combined with other peptides — its mechanism (upstream GnRH stimulation) doesn't have an established synergistic pairing in the way growth-hormone secretagogues are commonly combined.

Research and vendor-typical dosing centers around **100mcg** subcutaneous, though timing and frequency protocols vary considerably across research use and no formally validated general-use dosing schedule exists outside controlled clinical-research contexts like IVF ovulation triggering.

Given its mechanism of directly stimulating the **HPG axis**, theoretical concerns include effects on hormone-sensitive tissue and cycle disruption. Active hormone-sensitive cancers (prostate, breast) and pregnancy are treated as contraindications given the direct reproductive-hormone-axis mechanism. No comprehensive general-population safety data exists.

As an unmodified decapeptide, kisspeptin-10 is cleared rapidly from circulation — on the order of minutes — consistent with other small, unstabilized peptides. This short **half-life** is part of why clinical research uses continuous or repeated-pulse infusion protocols rather than single injections when studying sustained HPG-axis effects.

name: LL-37
subtitle: The human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide — part of the body's first line of defense against infection, studied for wound healing and immune modulation.
description: LL-37 is the human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, a 37-residue C-terminal fragment of the hCAP18 precursor protein, named for its first two residues (leucine-leucine) and total length. It's a cationic, amphipathic, alpha-helical peptide that disrupts bacterial cell membranes for broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, and plays a role in the body's innate immune response at sites of infection and inflammation. It's also studied for wound healing and angiogenesis. No established human clinical dosing protocol exists — nearly all substantive data is preclinical or in-vitro, and it's sold only as a research compound.

reconstitution.notes: A common research-vendor convention is a 5mg vial reconstituted with 2mL bacteriostatic water = 2500mcg/mL — this reflects vendor convention, not a validated clinical protocol.

halfLife: No formal human pharmacokinetic data published

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a research compound
Not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier D — real topical wound-gel RCTs exist (one small positive, one failed confirmatory), but the injectable form users buy has zero human data.
Strongest documented use case: antimicrobial and wound-healing activity as a host-defence peptide.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
A first-in-man venous-ulcer RCT (Grönberg 2014, N=34) healed faster than placebo, but the larger Phase IIb missed its primary endpoint.

sources.title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Human Antimicrobial Peptide LL-37
Immunomodulatory Functions of the Human Cathelicidin LL-37-Derived Peptides
Treatment with LL-37 is safe and effective in enhancing healing of hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers: a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial

sections.body: LL-37 is a **cationic**, amphipathic, alpha-helical peptide that inserts into and disrupts bacterial cell **membranes**, giving it broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. As part of the human **cathelicidin** family, it's produced by immune cells (neutrophils, macrophages) and epithelial cells as a first-line defense at sites of infection or injury.

Beyond directly killing pathogens, LL-37 is studied for roles in **wound healing** (promoting keratinocyte migration and angiogenesis) and broader **immunomodulation** — recruiting and activating other immune cells, and influencing inflammatory signaling at injury or infection sites.

The substantial majority of LL-37 research is preclinical — cell culture, animal models, and structural/biophysical studies of its membrane-disrupting mechanism. It's a well-studied molecule academically, but that depth of preclinical characterization has not translated into human clinical trials or an approved therapeutic use.

LL-37 has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of LL-37 in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

LL-37 doesn't have a well-established peptide-stacking pairing in the research-community sense — it's typically studied and used on its own for wound-healing or antimicrobial research angles, rather than combined into multi-peptide protocols.

There is **no established human clinical dosing protocol** for LL-37. Vendors sell it for topical and subcutaneous research use with wide, non-standardized ad hoc dosing conventions, but no formal human pharmacokinetic or dose-finding study has ever been published — treat any specific dose figure circulating in research communities as informal convention, not validated guidance.

No formal human safety or tolerability study exists for LL-37 administered as a standalone compound. Given its role in immune signaling, active **autoimmune conditions** are treated as a precautionary contraindication, along with pregnancy.

No formal human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for LL-37. Available data comes from in-vitro membrane-interaction studies and animal models rather than human plasma measurements.

name: VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide)
subtitle: A 28-amino-acid neuropeptide with broad vasodilator, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory effects, cleared from plasma within about a minute.
description: VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide) is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide that acts as a vasodilator, bronchodilator, and smooth-muscle relaxant, with additional anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties mediated through the VPAC1/VPAC2 receptors. It disappears from plasma extremely quickly after IV administration — a first-order half-time of about one minute — which is why intranasal and subcutaneous research routes are used to achieve more sustained local exposure. It's sold only as a research compound; no FDA approval exists for VIP itself.

reconstitution.notes: 5mg vial + 2mL bacteriostatic water = 2500mcg/mL for injectable use; intranasal kits are typically pre-formulated by the vendor.

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a research compound
Not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier C — human trials exist, but the lead programme did not carry through and there is no approval.
Strongest documented use case: investigational use of synthetic VIP (aviptadil) in respiratory failure.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Holds an orphan designation for ARDS, which is a regulatory status, not a demonstrated outcome.

sources.title: Vasoactive intestinal peptide in man: pharmacokinetics, metabolic and circulatory effects

sections.body: VIP binds **VPAC1** and **VPAC2** receptors distributed widely across the body — smooth muscle, immune cells, and the nervous system — producing **vasodilation**, bronchodilation, and smooth-muscle relaxation, alongside anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects. This broad receptor distribution is why VIP research spans cardiovascular, respiratory, and immune contexts rather than a single narrow application.

Beyond its vasoactive effects, VIP is studied for **neuroimmune** signaling — regulating cytokine production and immune cell activity in ways relevant to chronic inflammatory conditions. This has driven research interest in VIP for mold/biotoxin-illness and chronic inflammatory-response research protocols, though robust controlled human trial support for those specific applications is limited.

VIP's core physiology — vasodilation, bronchodilation, immune modulation — is well established from decades of basic-science and pharmacology research. However, its use as a therapeutic research compound for specific conditions (chronic inflammatory response, mold-illness protocols) rests on a much thinner and less rigorously controlled human evidence base.

VIP itself has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption** in the peptide-vendor research-chemical form sold to consumers. (Note: a related but chemically distinct VIP-based drug, aviptadil, has been separately studied for other indications — that is not the same product as research-grade VIP peptide.) It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of VIP in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.
VIP is typically used as a standalone compound in neuroimmune/inflammatory research protocols rather than combined with other peptides in an established stacking pattern.

Research protocols commonly cite **intranasal** dosing of 50-100mcg once or twice daily, and **subcutaneous** doses in the 50-300mcg range. These are informal research/vendor-protocol figures, not clinically validated doses — no formal human dose-finding trial has established a standard protocol for general research use.

Given its potent **vasodilator** mechanism, the main theoretical concern is transient **hypotension** or flushing, particularly with systemic (subcutaneous) administration. Formal adverse-event data at research-community dosing levels is limited. Pregnancy and active malignancy are treated as precautionary contraindications given the broad immunomodulatory mechanism.

After IV administration, plasma VIP levels fall by first-order kinetics with an average disappearance **half-time of about one minute** — one of the shortest half-lives of any peptide in this catalog. This extremely rapid systemic clearance is why intranasal and subcutaneous routes, which create more sustained local/regional exposure, are preferred in research use over IV.

name: AHK-Cu (Copper Tripeptide-3)
subtitle: A copper-binding tripeptide related to GHK-Cu, with research skewed toward hair-follicle and scalp effects rather than general skin remodeling.
description: AHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-3) is a copper-binding tripeptide — alanine-histidine-lysine complexed with a copper ion — structurally related to the better-known GHK-Cu but studied with a research emphasis on hair-follicle and dermal-papilla stimulation rather than general skin remodeling. Its regulatory situation has two distinct halves: cosmetic-grade topical AHK-Cu, sold in serums and scalp products, is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient and doesn't require premarket drug approval. Injectable or microneedling-delivered AHK-Cu sold by research-peptide vendors is a separate, unapproved research chemical, not intended for human use.
