reconstitution.notes: For the injectable/research vial form: a common convention is a 50mg vial + 5mL bacteriostatic water. Topical cosmetic products require no reconstitution.

contraindications: known copper sensitivity or Wilson's disease

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a cosmetic ingredient (topical) or research compound (injectable)
Topical form: regulated as a cosmetic ingredient, no premarket approval required. Injectable/research form: not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier D — in-vitro and small cosmetic studies only, with no controlled clinical outcome.
Strongest documented use case: topical copper delivery for hair and skin, mostly from manufacturer-run testing.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Distinct from GHK-Cu despite the shared copper chemistry — the evidence does not carry across.

sources.title: The effect of tripeptide-copper complex on human hair growth in vitro

sections.body: AHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide (Ala-His-Lys complexed with **Cu2+**), structurally distinct from **GHK-Cu** despite the similar naming convention and shared copper-peptide category. Where GHK-Cu's research base is broad (skin remodeling, wound healing, collagen synthesis), AHK-Cu's research is more specifically oriented toward **hair follicle** and scalp effects.

sections.subheader: Dermal Papilla and Growth Factor Signaling
sections.body: Research on AHK-Cu centers on stimulation of **dermal papilla cells** — the signaling hub at the base of hair follicles that regulates the hair growth cycle — alongside collagen synthesis and general tissue-regeneration effects broadly similar in category to copper-peptide biology overall, driven by copper-dependent upregulation of growth factors and matrix remodeling.

Most published evidence on AHK-Cu comes from cosmetic-industry and in-vitro dermal-papilla-cell research, funded largely by cosmetic ingredient suppliers, rather than independent clinical trials. This is a different evidence pathway than pharmaceutical drug development, and claims should be weighed accordingly — a cosmetic ingredient can be legally marketed without FDA drug-style efficacy trials.

AHK-Cu's legal status depends entirely on the **form** sold. **Topical** AHK-Cu, used in cosmetic serums and scalp products, is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient and does not require FDA premarket drug approval. **Injectable or microneedling-delivered** AHK-Cu, sold by research-peptide vendors, is a separate, unapproved research chemical — **not approved for human use** in that form, and sold RUO. Don't conflate the two: a legally-sold cosmetic serum and an unapproved injectable research vial are regulated completely differently.

AHK-Cu is commonly paired with **GHK-Cu** in skin and hair research protocols — combining AHK-Cu's hair-follicle-oriented research with GHK-Cu's broader, better-studied skin-remodeling and collagen effects.

**Topical** cosmetic serums specify a formulated **concentration** rather than an injectable dose, applied per product label directions. For the **injectable/research vial** form sold by peptide vendors, no standardized clinical dose exists — informal research protocols vary considerably vendor to vendor.

Topical cosmetic use is generally well tolerated, with rare mild skin irritation reported. The injectable/research form carries the same general uncharacterized-risk profile as other unapproved research peptides — no formal human safety trial exists for that route. Known copper-metabolism disorders (e.g. **Wilson's disease**) and pregnancy are treated as precautionary contraindications for the injectable/research form.

No formal human pharmacokinetic study exists for AHK-Cu in either form. Topical use is designed for local, not systemic, exposure, so a conventional plasma **half-life** isn't the relevant metric; for the injectable/research form, systemic pharmacokinetics remain uncharacterized.

name: KLOW Blend
subtitle: A single-vial 4-peptide blend combining GHK-Cu, KPV, BPC-157, and TB-500 — the most comprehensive of the popular research recovery blends.
description: A single-vial blend combining GHK-Cu (skin/collagen remodeling), KPV (anti-inflammatory, gut and skin support), BPC-157 (soft-tissue and gut healing), and TB-500 (systemic tissue repair and angiogenesis) — the most comprehensive of the popular multi-peptide recovery blends, one injection covering skin, gut, and connective-tissue research angles at once.

reconstitution.notes: Most commonly sold as an 80mg vial (50mg GHK-Cu, 10mg KPV, 10mg BPC-157, 10mg TB-500); reconstitute with 3.0mL bacteriostatic water for roughly 26.7mg/mL total blend concentration. Ratios vary by supplier.

quickFacts.value: Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier B — observational human data (cohort / case studies).
Strongest documented use case: Joint, Gut & Skin Recovery.
1 tracked outcome area with graded citations.
Classified as: 4-peptide clinic blend: GHK-Cu + KPV + BPC-157 + TB-500.

evidenceClaims.note: no trial of the 4-peptide combination; half its components are preclinical-only

sections.body: KLOW combines four peptides that individually target overlapping-but-distinct repair pathways: **GHK-Cu** upregulates collagen, elastin, and angiogenic growth-factor expression for skin/connective-tissue remodeling; **KPV** carries anti-inflammatory melanocortin signaling without pigmentation effects; **BPC-157** shows gastroprotective and soft-tissue repair activity through nitric-oxide signaling and growth-factor modulation; **TB-500** promotes cell migration and angiogenesis via actin-sequestering pathways. Combined, the blend targets skin, gut, and connective-tissue repair simultaneously.

KLOW is most commonly sold as an **80mg vial** containing **50mg GHK-Cu, 10mg KPV, 10mg BPC-157, and 10mg TB-500** — GHK-Cu dominates the formulation by mass, with the other three peptides present at equal, smaller doses. Exact ratios vary by supplier, so always confirm the specific vial's composition before dosing.

sections.subheader: Individually Studied, Never Combined in a Trial
sections.body: Each of KLOW's four components has its own body of preclinical and observational research individually. No clinical trial has ever tested the **4-peptide combination itself** — the blend's rationale rests on combining individually-plausible mechanisms, not on trial data for the combination as a product.

KLOW is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound and is **not approved for human consumption** by the FDA or any equivalent regulatory body. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of KLOW and its individual component peptides in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

KLOW is designed as a comprehensive standalone recovery blend rather than a component of a larger stack — it already combines four peptides in one vial. Some researchers still pair it with **GH secretagogue blends** (e.g. CJC-1295 no-DAC + Ipamorelin) for broader systemic recovery support alongside KLOW's localized tissue-repair focus.

Clinics commonly dose KLOW by its **GHK-Cu content** — roughly 1–2mg GHK-Cu equivalent per injection, which works out to about 16–32 units on a U-100 insulin syringe after standard reconstitution. Typical total-blend doses run **250–750mcg daily**. Reconstitute the 80mg vial with **3.0mL bacteriostatic water** for a concentration of about 26.7mg/mL total blend (vendor protocols range 1–3mL). Cycles commonly run **4–12 weeks**.

Because KLOW combines four separately-acting peptides, its side-effect profile reflects the union of each component's known/theoretical risks — mild injection-site irritation, and (from the BPC-157/TB-500 pairing) the standard soft-tissue-repair-peptide caution around active malignancy given their angiogenic and cell-migration-promoting mechanisms. No formal combined-product safety trial exists.

KLOW's four components have distinct individual pharmacokinetic profiles and are not expected to share a single **half-life** — there is no published pharmacokinetic study of the combined blend as a product. Reconstituted KLOW should be refrigerated and used within the timeframe recommended by the specific vendor, consistent with standard peptide-blend handling practice.

name: GLOW Blend
subtitle: A copper-peptide-forward single-vial blend pairing GHK-Cu's skin remodeling with BPC-157 and TB-500's tissue-repair support.
description: GLOW pairs GHK-Cu's skin-remodeling and collagen-stimulating effects with BPC-157 and TB-500's tissue-repair support in a single vial — positioned by vendors as the skin-forward counterpart to the more recovery-focused KLOW blend, which adds KPV for gut/anti-inflammatory coverage that GLOW leaves out in favor of a higher relative GHK-Cu dose.

quickFacts.value: Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier B — observational human data (cohort / case studies).
Strongest documented use case: Skin & Connective Tissue.
1 tracked outcome area with graded citations.
Classified as: clinic blend: GHK-Cu + BPC-157 + TB-500.

evidenceClaims.note: anchored on GHK-Cu's human cosmetic literature; no trial of the blend itself

sections.body: GLOW combines **GHK-Cu** (dosed as the majority component by mass) with smaller equal doses of **BPC-157** and **TB-500**. GHK-Cu drives collagen, elastin, and angiogenic growth-factor upregulation for skin remodeling; BPC-157 and TB-500 contribute gastroprotective, soft-tissue-repair, and angiogenic support. The higher relative GHK-Cu dose is what gives GLOW its skin-forward positioning compared to KLOW.
GLOW is most commonly sold as a **70mg vial** containing **50mg GHK-Cu, 10mg BPC-157, and 10mg TB-500** — a 5:1:1 ratio by mass. This is the same three-peptide combination found in KLOW, minus KPV.

sections.subheader: Individually Studied, Never Combined in a Trial
sections.body: As with other multi-peptide vendor blends, each of GLOW's three components has its own individual research base, but no clinical trial has tested the **3-peptide combination** itself as a product.

GLOW is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound and is **not approved for human consumption** by the FDA or any equivalent regulatory body. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of GLOW and its individual component peptides in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

GLOW is designed as a standalone skin-and-recovery blend. Some researchers pair it with standalone **AHK-Cu** for combined hair/skin research coverage, or with GH secretagogue blends for broader systemic recovery support alongside GLOW's skin-focused mechanism.

Reconstitute the 70mg vial with **3.0mL bacteriostatic water** for a concentration of about 23.3mg/mL total blend. A typical daily dose is **~2.33mg (2,330mcg)** total blend, delivering roughly 1.7mg GHK-Cu, 0.33mg TB-500, and 0.33mg BPC-157 per injection. Cycles commonly run **4–8 weeks**.

GLOW's side-effect profile reflects the union of its three components' known/theoretical risks — mild injection-site irritation, and the standard caution around active malignancy given BPC-157 and TB-500's angiogenic and cell-migration-promoting mechanisms. No formal combined-product safety trial exists.

GLOW's three components have distinct individual pharmacokinetic profiles rather than a single blend-wide **half-life** — no published pharmacokinetic study exists for the combined product. Reconstituted GLOW should be refrigerated and used within the vendor's recommended window.

name: Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin Blend
subtitle: A single-vial blend pairing FDA-approved GHRH analog Tesamorelin with the selective ghrelin-agonist Ipamorelin for a combined GH pulse in one injection.
description: A single-vial blend pairing Tesamorelin — a GHRH analog FDA-approved as Egrifta for HIV-associated lipodystrophy and widely used off-label for GH-axis support — with Ipamorelin, a selective ghrelin-receptor-agonist GH secretagogue. Same combined-mechanism logic as the existing CJC-1295 (no-DAC) + Ipamorelin blend, using Tesamorelin as the GHRH-analog half instead of CJC-1295.

quickFacts.value: Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier B — observational human data (cohort / case studies).
Strongest documented use case: GH Axis Support.
1 tracked outcome area with graded citations.
Classified as: clinic blend: Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin.

evidenceClaims.note: anchored on tesamorelin's FDA-approved GH-axis data; no trial of the combination

sections.body: **Tesamorelin** is a GHRH analog that stimulates the pituitary's own **GHRH receptor** to release growth hormone in a physiological, pulsatile pattern — it's the only FDA-approved compound in this combination, approved as Egrifta for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. **Ipamorelin** works through a separate receptor, the **ghrelin receptor**, triggering an independent GH pulse. Hitting both receptors at once is the same combined-mechanism logic behind REGEN's existing CJC-1295 (no-DAC) + Ipamorelin blend, substituting Tesamorelin as the GHRH-analog half.

sections.subheader: Why Pair a GHRH Analog with a Ghrelin Agonist
sections.body: Because **GHRH** and **ghrelin** signal through distinct pituitary receptor pathways, combining an analog of each produces a larger GH pulse than either alone — a well-established pharmacological principle in GH secretagogue research, though it doesn't guarantee proportionally larger downstream benefits without dedicated combination-trial data.

sections.subheader: Strong Individual Data, No Combination Trial
sections.body: Tesamorelin has the strongest evidence base of any compound in REGEN's GH-secretagogue category — it's **FDA-approved** based on multiple Phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in HIV-associated lipodystrophy. Ipamorelin has solid mechanistic and animal/early human pharmacology data as a selective ghrelin-receptor agonist. Neither compound, however, has been studied **in combination** in a controlled trial — the blend's rationale rests on complementary receptor mechanisms, not combination-specific trial data.

This blend is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound and is **not approved for human consumption** as a combined product — Tesamorelin itself is FDA-approved as Egrifta for a specific indication, but the combined blend sold by research-peptide vendors is not an FDA-approved product. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of this blend in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

sections.subheader: An Alternative to the CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin Blend
sections.body: This blend serves a similar role to REGEN's existing **CJC-1295 (no-DAC) + Ipamorelin blend**, and researchers generally choose one or the other rather than combining both — Tesamorelin's FDA-approval history gives it the stronger individual safety/efficacy record, while CJC-1295 (no-DAC) has a shorter, more classically "pulsatile" pharmacokinetic profile.

Following each component's individual standard dosing: **Tesamorelin 1–2mg** subcutaneous once daily, and **Ipamorelin 200–300mcg** subcutaneous 1–3x daily. As with the CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin blend, dosing is typically timed around fasted states (e.g. pre-bed) to align with the body's natural nighttime GH pulse.

Tesamorelin's FDA label documents injection-site reactions, joint pain/arthralgia, and peripheral edema as the most common effects, plus a mild reduction in glucose tolerance in some patients — worth monitoring via **fasting glucose**/**HbA1c**. Ipamorelin's ghrelin-receptor mechanism is generally considered the most selective (fewest off-target effects) among GH secretagogues. Active malignancy and pregnancy are contraindicated given the GH/IGF-1 axis stimulation shared by both components.

Tesamorelin and Ipamorelin clear independently rather than sharing a unified **half-life** — no published pharmacokinetic study exists for the combined blend as a product, only for each compound individually.

name: Oxytocin
subtitle: A naturally occurring nonapeptide — FDA-approved as Pitocin for labor, and separately studied off-label (intranasal) for social bonding and stress research.
description: Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid neuropeptide produced in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary, best known for its roles in labor, lactation, and social bonding. Its synthetic form is FDA-approved (as Pitocin/Syntocinon) for inducing labor and managing postpartum hemorrhage — a well-established, decades-old obstetric drug. Separately, intranasal oxytocin has become a popular research and self-experimentation compound for social bonding, trust, and stress-response research, an application that is not FDA-approved and rests on a much thinner evidence base than its obstetric use.

reconstitution.notes: Injectable/research vial form: a common convention is a 10mg (≈300 IU) vial reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Intranasal research kits are typically pre-formulated by the vendor at a fixed IU/spray concentration.

quickFacts.value: Prescription-only, FDA-approved for labor induction/postpartum hemorrhage. Intranasal use for social/bonding research is not FDA-approved for that purpose — sold RUO
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier B — a real FDA approval (Pitocin), but for an unrelated indication by a different route.
Strongest documented use case: induction and augmentation of labour by intravenous infusion.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
The intranasal social-cognition literature is large but has replicated poorly, and is a separate question from the approval.

sections.body: **Oxytocin** binds oxytocin receptors in the uterus, mammary gland, and brain. In the uterus, receptor activation drives smooth-muscle contraction — the basis for its **FDA-approved** obstetric use (labor induction, controlling postpartum bleeding). In the brain, oxytocin signaling is implicated in social bonding, trust, and stress-response modulation — a completely separate research application from its clinical drug use.

Because oxytocin doesn't cross the **blood-brain barrier** efficiently when given IV/IM (the route used for labor), the social/bonding research literature relies almost entirely on **intranasal** administration, which is thought to reach the brain more directly via the olfactory and trigeminal pathways — a distinct route and distinct evidence base from the obstetric drug.

sections.subheader: Well-Established Obstetric Use, Thinner Behavioral Evidence
sections.body: Oxytocin's obstetric use is one of the oldest, most established indications in modern pharmacology. Its use for **social bonding**, trust, and anxiety research is a much newer and more mixed literature — hundreds of small studies exist, but replication has been inconsistent, and effect sizes are often modest.

Synthetic oxytocin is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved** as Pitocin/Syntocinon for labor induction and postpartum hemorrhage management. **Intranasal** oxytocin used for social/bonding/stress research is **not FDA-approved** for that purpose and is sold by research-peptide vendors as an unapproved compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of intranasal/research-use oxytocin in their jurisdiction prior to use.
Oxytocin is typically used as a standalone compound in bonding/stress research rather than combined with other peptides in an established stacking protocol.

Research protocols commonly cite **20–40 IU** intranasal, with 24 IU (6 sprays at 4 IU/spray) a frequently cited standard dose, administered 30–45 minutes before the target activity. Effects are reported to begin within 15–30 minutes and last roughly 2–4 hours. This is informal research-community convention, not an FDA-approved dosing schedule — the FDA-approved Pitocin dosing (for labor) is a completely separate, clinically-titrated IV protocol.

Clinical IV/IM Pitocin use carries well-characterized risks around uterine hyperstimulation and fluid balance, managed under direct medical supervision during labor. Intranasal research use has a much thinner safety record; commonly reported effects are mild — nasal irritation, mild headache — but comprehensive safety data at research-community dosing levels doesn't exist. Significant cardiovascular disease is a precautionary contraindication given oxytocin's effects on vascular tone.

Oxytocin has a plasma **half-life** of roughly 3–5 minutes, rapidly broken down by the enzyme oxytocinase. This very short half-life is why IV administration for labor requires a continuous infusion rather than a single bolus, and why intranasal research protocols are timed shortly before the activity of interest.

name: Pinealon
subtitle: A Khavinson-group tripeptide bioregulator, studied preclinically for neuroprotective and cognitive-aging effects.
description: Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg, abbreviated EDR) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's research group in St. Petersburg — the same lab behind Epithalon. It belongs to a family of short 'peptide bioregulators' the group proposes act by binding DNA promoter regions to modulate gene transcription, a mechanistic hypothesis that remains contested outside that research tradition. Pinealon is studied primarily in preclinical/animal models for neuroprotective and cognitive-aging effects. It's sold only as a research compound; no FDA approval or large human trial exists.

reconstitution.notes: 20mg vial + 2mL bacteriostatic water = 10,000mcg/mL.

halfLife: Expected on the order of minutes (unmodified short peptide) — no direct human plasma half-life study has been published

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — sold as a research compound
Not FDA-approved for human use — research use only (RUO)
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

evidenceSummary: REGEN Research Tier F — no independent human evidence — a peptide bioregulator sold ahead of its data.
Strongest documented use case: claimed neuroprotection, unsupported by controlled trials.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.
Shares its origin and its evidence problem with Epithalon.

sections.body: Pinealon (**EDR**: Glu-Asp-Arg) is a synthetic tripeptide from the same research tradition as **Epithalon** — the 'peptide bioregulator' family developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group. The proposed mechanism is that short peptides like EDR bind complementarily to **DNA promoter regions**, modulating gene transcription directly — a hypothesis distinct from the receptor-agonist mechanisms most peptides in this catalog use, and one that remains contested and unreplicated outside the originating research group.

Pinealon-specific research centers on **neuroprotective** and cognitive-aging effects in animal models, positioned within the Khavinson group's broader work on organ-specific 'bioregulator' peptides (Pinealon for brain/pineal tissue, similar to how their other tripeptides target other organ systems).

Nearly all published Pinealon research originates from the Khavinson group and affiliated Russian institutions, using older publication standards and small sample sizes, mostly in animal models. Independent replication outside this research tradition is minimal, and no modern, controlled human trial exists.

Pinealon has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of Pinealon in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

Pinealon is frequently sold and used alongside **Epithalon** and **DSIP** in longevity/circadian research protocols — all three come from short-peptide or sleep-regulatory research traditions and are commonly bundled by vendors as a combo. No formal trial data exists for any combination.

Vendor/research-typical dosing mirrors the Epithalon convention: **5–10mg daily** subcutaneous or intranasal for a **10–20 day course**, cycled rather than used continuously. This comes from the originating research group's protocol design, not a formal human dose-finding trial.

No formal human safety or tolerability data exists for Pinealon at scale. Pregnancy and active malignancy are treated as precautionary contraindications, consistent with other short bioregulator peptides in this catalog with a similarly thin safety record.

No study has directly measured Pinealon's plasma **half-life** in humans. Based on the general pharmacokinetics of short, unmodified peptides, its circulating half-life is expected to be on the order of minutes — an extrapolation, not a confirmed measurement.

name: Thymosin Alpha-1
subtitle: A 28-amino-acid thymic peptide approved in 35+ countries as Zadaxin for immune support — but never FDA-approved in the United States.
description: Thymosin Alpha-1 is a naturally occurring 28-amino-acid peptide fragment of prothymosin alpha, produced by the thymus gland and involved in T-cell maturation and innate immune signaling (notably through TLR9). Under the brand name Zadaxin, it's an approved drug in more than 35 countries — including Italy and China — for chronic hepatitis B and C and as a general immune-modulating agent. It has never been FDA-approved in the United States; as of a February 2026 reclassification, it holds FDA 503A Category 2 status, meaning US patients can access it only by prescription through licensed compounding pharmacies.

reconstitution.notes: 1.6mg vial reconstituted with 1mL bacteriostatic water per the Zadaxin clinical dosing convention, where available.

contraindications: organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy

quickFacts.value: Zadaxin (approved in 35+ countries; not FDA-approved in the US)
Not FDA-approved in the US. FDA 503A Category 2 status (Feb 2026) — prescription-only via licensed compounding pharmacies
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

Strongest documented use case: adjunct treatment of chronic hepatitis B and C.
No graded outcome areas recorded yet — tier assigned from regulatory and published-trial status.

sections.body: **Thymosin Alpha-1** is a fragment of prothymosin alpha, naturally produced by the thymus gland, where it plays a role in **T-cell** maturation and differentiation. It also acts as a **TLR9** (Toll-like receptor 9) agonist, engaging innate immune pathways — a dual innate/adaptive immune-signaling profile that underlies its use as a general immune-modulating agent.

Because it touches both innate and adaptive immunity, Thymosin Alpha-1 has been studied across a wide range of applications — chronic viral hepatitis, as an adjunct to vaccines and cancer immunotherapy, and general immune support — rather than one narrow mechanism-to-outcome pathway.

sections.subheader: Approved Abroad, Not in the US
sections.body: As **Zadaxin**, Thymosin Alpha-1 is an approved drug in more than **35 countries** — including Italy, China, South Korea, and India — for chronic **hepatitis B and C** and as an immunomodulatory agent, with decades of international clinical use and post-marketing data. It has never completed FDA approval in the United States.

Thymosin Alpha-1 is **not FDA-approved** in the US. As of a **February 2026 reclassification**, it holds **FDA 503A Category 2** status, meaning it can legally be dispensed in the US only by prescription through a **licensed compounding pharmacy** — a different (and more regulated) pathway than an unapproved research chemical, but still short of full FDA drug approval. Verify any US source is a licensed compounding pharmacy operating under a valid prescription.

Thymosin Alpha-1 is typically used as a standalone immune-support compound, sometimes alongside standard-of-care treatment for chronic viral hepatitis in countries where it's approved, rather than combined with other peptides in a stacking protocol.

Where Zadaxin is approved, standard dosing is **1.6mg** subcutaneous **twice weekly**. This is the most widely cited protocol in both clinical and research-vendor contexts, reflecting the international drug's actual approved label dosing rather than an informal research-community estimate.

Given decades of use as an approved drug abroad, Thymosin Alpha-1 has a comparatively well-characterized safety profile for a peptide in this catalog — commonly reported effects include mild injection-site irritation. As an immune-activating compound, it's contraindicated in **organ transplant recipients** on immunosuppressive therapy (it could counteract the immunosuppression) and treated with caution in autoimmune conditions. Pregnancy is a precautionary contraindication.

Thymosin Alpha-1 has a plasma **half-life** of approximately 2 hours, though its immunomodulatory effects — driven by downstream immune-cell signaling rather than sustained receptor occupancy — persist well beyond the compound's direct circulating presence, consistent with its twice-weekly clinical dosing schedule.

name: Larazotide
subtitle: An oral zonulin antagonist that holds the gut's tight junctions shut against gluten — a celiac-disease drug candidate, not a general gut-health peptide.
description: Larazotide is an oral octapeptide zonulin antagonist, designed to tighten the gut's paracellular tight junctions and block the intestinal permeability response triggered by gluten in celiac disease. A positive Phase 2 trial (0.5mg three times daily) reduced persistent celiac symptoms, but the pivotal Phase 3 trial, CeDLara, was terminated in 2022 after a futility interim analysis, and the development program was discontinued. There is no evidence supporting its use for general 'leaky gut' or gut-health claims outside celiac disease specifically.
halfLife: Not established — designed to act locally in the gut lumen rather than systemically

quickFacts.value: No trademarked brand — clinical development discontinued before reaching market
Not FDA-approved — Phase 3 program (CeDLara) terminated in 2022. Sold RUO
Room temperature, sealed, away from light and moisture. No refrigeration or reconstitution required.

sections.body: Larazotide is a **zonulin antagonist** — zonulin is the endogenous signal that loosens the tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells, and gluten exposure triggers excess zonulin release in people with celiac disease. By blocking this pathway, larazotide is designed to keep the gut's **tight junctions** shut, limiting the permeability spike (and downstream immune activation) that gluten exposure causes.

sections.subheader: A Celiac Drug, Not a General Gut-Health Peptide
sections.body: Larazotide acts locally in the gut lumen rather than being systemically absorbed, which is part of its safety appeal as an oral drug candidate. Critically, it was developed and studied specifically for **celiac disease** — there is no evidence it addresses general 'leaky gut' or non-celiac gut-health concerns, despite how it's sometimes marketed.

sections.subheader: A Positive Phase 2 That Didn't Carry Through
sections.body: In a 2015 Phase 2 trial (Leffler et al., **Gastroenterology**, n=342), larazotide at 0.5mg three times daily reduced persistent celiac symptoms compared to placebo in patients already on a gluten-free diet — notably, higher doses performed no better. This positive signal supported advancement to Phase 3.

sections.subheader: Phase 3 Termination and Regulatory and Legal Status
sections.body: The pivotal Phase 3 trial, **CeDLara**, was terminated in 2022 at a pre-planned futility interim analysis — it could not reach statistical significance, and the development program was discontinued. Larazotide is **not FDA-approved** and has no path to market as things stand. It is sold today only as a research-grade compound (RUO); researchers and users should verify the legal status of larazotide in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.

Larazotide is studied and used as a standalone gut-barrier compound rather than combined with other peptides — its mechanism (local tight-junction modulation) doesn't have an established synergistic pairing with systemic peptides like BPC-157.

The only dose with meaningful supporting data is **0.5mg orally, three times daily** — the regimen used in the positive Phase 2 trial. Higher doses tested in the same trial showed no additional benefit. No FDA-approved or otherwise validated dosing schedule exists beyond this trial protocol.

Larazotide acts locally in the gut and is minimally systemically absorbed, which is part of why it was generally well-tolerated in trials, with mild GI effects (bloating, discomfort) most commonly reported. Comprehensive long-term safety data beyond the discontinued trial program doesn't exist.

sections.subheader: Designed for Local, Not Systemic, Action
sections.body: Larazotide's mechanism depends on acting locally within the gut lumen at the tight-junction level, rather than systemic absorption and circulation — a conventional plasma **half-life** isn't the relevant pharmacokinetic parameter here the way it is for injectable peptides.

name: SS-31 (Elamipretide)
subtitle: A mitochondria-targeting tetrapeptide, FDA-approved in September 2025 for Barth syndrome — a real approval in one narrow rare disease, not a general muscle or longevity drug.
description: SS-31 (elamipretide) is a small, mitochondria-targeting tetrapeptide that concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and stabilizes cardiolipin, a lipid essential to mitochondrial energy production. It received FDA approval in September 2025 for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited mitochondrial muscle disease, after an extension study showed meaningful improvement in a 6-minute walk test. That approval is genuinely narrow, though: a larger 218-person trial in a different mitochondrial-muscle condition (MMPOWER-3) showed no improvement in walking distance or fatigue, and separate heart-failure and dry-AMD trials both missed their primary endpoints. It's grouped with longevity research because of its mitochondrial mechanism, but that broader case rests mostly on animal data plus this one rare-disease approval.

standardDose.frequency: 1x daily (subcutaneous, as approved for Barth syndrome)

reconstitution.notes: Research-vendor convention: 40mg vial reconstituted with 2mL bacteriostatic water. The FDA-approved Barth syndrome product is a pre-filled subcutaneous formulation, not a lyophilized research vial.

quickFacts.value: FDA-approved for Barth syndrome (Sept 2025) — general research-vendor form has no trademarked brand
FDA-approved for Barth syndrome specifically; general/off-label research use is not FDA-approved for that purpose — sold RUO outside the approved indication
Store the lyophilized vial refrigerated (2-8°C) or at -20°C, away from light. Once reconstituted, keep refrigerated at 2-8°C and use promptly.

Strongest documented use case: mitochondrial muscle function in Barth syndrome specifically.

sections.body: SS-31 is a small, positively-charged tetrapeptide that selectively concentrates in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**, where it binds and stabilizes **cardiolipin** — a lipid essential to the structure of the electron transport chain and efficient ATP production. Stabilizing cardiolipin is thought to reduce electron leakage and reactive oxygen species production in dysfunctional mitochondria.

SS-31 (as elamipretide) received **FDA approval in September 2025** specifically for **Barth syndrome**, a rare inherited mitochondrial disease causing muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. This is a genuine regulatory approval, not a research-community claim — but it applies to one narrow, rare population, not muscle function or mitochondrial health broadly.

sections.subheader: A Real Win, With a Real Miss Right Next to It
sections.body: The **TAZPOWER** extension study tracked 8 Barth syndrome patients out to 168 weeks and saw them walk roughly 96 meters farther on a 6-minute walk test — the data that supported FDA approval. But **MMPOWER-3**, a larger 218-person, 24-week trial in a different mitochondrial-muscle condition, saw no improvement in walking distance or fatigue. Separately, heart-failure and dry age-related macular degeneration trials both missed their primary endpoints. The win is real but genuinely narrow.

SS-31 is **FDA-approved** specifically for Barth syndrome as of September 2025. Use outside that approved indication — including general mitochondrial-health or longevity research use — is **not FDA-approved** for that purpose, and is sold by research-peptide vendors as an unapproved compound (RUO) in that context. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of off-label SS-31 use in their jurisdiction.

SS-31 is typically studied and used standalone, targeting mitochondrial function specifically. It's sometimes discussed alongside other mitochondrial-derived peptides like **MOTS-c** or **Humanin** in longevity research contexts, though no formal combination trial data exists for any pairing.

The FDA-approved Barth syndrome regimen uses a pre-filled subcutaneous formulation dosed daily; research-vendor protocols commonly cite around **40mg subcutaneous daily** from a reconstituted vial, mirroring the approved dose. Outside the approved indication, there's no validated dose-finding data to guide use.

In the Barth syndrome trial program, injection-site reactions were the most commonly reported effect. Given the mixed results across other trial populations (heart failure, dry AMD, the broader mitochondrial-muscle trial), comprehensive safety data outside the approved rare-disease population remains limited.

SS-31 has a plasma **half-life** of roughly 7-10 hours, but its relevant pharmacology is really about mitochondrial concentration rather than plasma persistence — it accumulates selectively in mitochondria-dense tissue (heart, skeletal muscle) far above plasma levels.

name: Melanotan I (Afamelanotide)
subtitle: The only melanotan with FDA approval — cleared as Scenesse in 2019 for a rare disorder where sunlight causes severe skin pain, not for general tanning.
description: Melanotan I (afamelanotide) is an alpha-MSH analog that, unlike Melanotan II, targets only the MC1R (melanocortin-1) pigment receptor — which is why it lacks the libido and appetite effects seen with Melanotan II's broader receptor activity. It's the only compound in the melanotan family with real FDA approval: cleared in 2019 under the brand Scenesse as a subcutaneous implant for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare disorder in which sunlight exposure causes severe skin pain. A 2015 vitiligo trial also showed it improved repigmentation when combined with phototherapy. That approval is narrow — using it for general tanning or cosmetic purposes sits outside what was actually tested and approved.

reconstitution.notes: Research-vendor convention: 10mg vial reconstituted with 2mL bacteriostatic water. The FDA-approved Scenesse product is a subcutaneous implant, not an injectable vial.

contraindications: known photosensitizing conditions requiring specialist oversight

sections.body: Melanotan I (afamelanotide) activates only the **MC1R** (melanocortin-1 receptor), the pigment-specific receptor that drives melanin production in skin. This is the key structural/functional difference from **Melanotan II**, which activates MC1R alongside MC3R and MC4R — receptors responsible for appetite and sexual-arousal effects. By targeting MC1R alone, afamelanotide produces skin darkening and photoprotection without those broader systemic effects.

Increased **melanin** production provides genuine photoprotective benefit by absorbing and dissipating UV and visible-light energy before it damages skin cells — the basis for its approved use in **erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)**, where accumulated porphyrins make even normal light exposure intensely painful.

Afamelanotide was **FDA-approved in 2019** under the brand **Scenesse** — a subcutaneous implant — specifically for erythropoietic protoporphyria, where it meaningfully increases pain-free light exposure time for patients. Separately, a 2015 trial (Lim et al., **JAMA Dermatology**, n=55) found monthly afamelanotide added to narrowband UVB phototherapy improved vitiligo repigmentation compared to phototherapy alone, with a larger effect in darker skin tones.

Melanotan I is **FDA-approved** as Scenesse specifically for EPP. Use for general tanning or cosmetic purposes is **not** what was tested or approved — that use is off-label at best, and unapproved research-chemical use in that context should be treated as RUO. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of non-EPP afamelanotide use in their jurisdiction.

Melanotan I is used as a standalone photoprotection/pigmentation compound. Unlike Melanotan II, it isn't typically discussed as part of a sexual-health or appetite-related stacking protocol, since it lacks those receptor targets entirely.

The FDA-approved Scenesse product is a **16mg subcutaneous implant** administered roughly monthly by a healthcare provider. Research-vendor vials are commonly reconstituted and dosed in smaller increments (research-typical protocols vary considerably) — this does not replicate the approved implant's controlled, sustained-release delivery.

Because it doesn't activate MC3R/MC4R, Melanotan I lacks the nausea, flushing, and spontaneous erection side effects commonly reported with **Melanotan II**. Implant-site reactions and headache are the most commonly reported effects in the Scenesse trial program. Active malignancy is a precautionary contraindication given the melanocyte-stimulating mechanism.

sections.subheader: Short Circulating Half-Life, Implant Extends Duration
sections.body: Free afamelanotide has a short plasma **half-life** of roughly 30-50 minutes; the FDA-approved implant achieves its roughly month-long duration of effect through sustained-release delivery from the implant itself, not from the peptide's intrinsic pharmacokinetics.

name: 5-Amino-1MQ
subtitle: An NNMT-inhibiting small molecule studied for fat loss in obese mice — no human trials have been published as of 2026.
description: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small-molecule inhibitor of NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase), an enzyme that helps fat cells store energy and that's been linked to obesity and metabolic dysfunction. In diet-induced-obese mice, blocking NNMT with 5-Amino-1MQ cut body weight by roughly 7%. It is not a peptide — it's a small molecule, popular in the same longevity/fat-loss research circles as NAD+ and MOTS-c. As of 2026, all efficacy evidence is animal-only; no human trial has been published.

sections.subheader: Blocking NNMT to Change Fat-Cell Metabolism
sections.body: 5-Amino-1MQ inhibits **NNMT** (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase), an enzyme highly expressed in fat tissue that methylates nicotinamide, consuming a methyl-donor pool the cell would otherwise use for other metabolic processes. NNMT activity has been linked to fat-cell energy storage and to obesity in human observational data, which is the rationale for studying its inhibition as a fat-loss strategy.

Unlike most compounds in this catalog, 5-Amino-1MQ is a **small molecule**, not a peptide — structurally unrelated to amino-acid chains. It's grouped in the same research-vendor and longevity-community conversation as NAD+ and MOTS-c because of shared interest in metabolic/mitochondrial health, not because of any structural similarity.

The primary supporting study (Neelakantan et al., 2018, **Bioorg Med Chem Lett**) showed that blocking NNMT with 5-Amino-1MQ reduced body weight by roughly 7% and lowered white-fat mass in a diet-induced-obesity mouse model. As of 2026, **no human trial** of 5-Amino-1MQ has been published — the entire efficacy case rests on this and related animal extrapolation.

5-Amino-1MQ is **not FDA-approved** for any indication and is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of 5-Amino-1MQ in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use, and should weigh the complete absence of human trial data accordingly.

5-Amino-1MQ is frequently sold and used alongside **NAD+** and **MOTS-c** in longevity/metabolic-health research protocols — all three are positioned around cellular energy metabolism, though no formal trial data exists for any combination.

Research-vendor products are commonly dosed at **50–150mg** orally once daily. Since no human trial exists, this range reflects informal research-community convention extrapolated from animal dosing, not a validated human dose-finding study.

Because no human trial has been published, there is no characterized human side-effect profile for 5-Amino-1MQ. Active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication given NNMT's broader role in cellular methylation metabolism, which has documented links to some cancer biology in unrelated research contexts.

No human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for 5-Amino-1MQ. All available PK-adjacent data comes from the mouse model in the foundational efficacy study.

name: Gonadorelin
subtitle: A synthetic copy of GnRH, the body's own upstream trigger for testosterone — used by TRT clinics to keep the testes active during therapy.
description: Gonadorelin is a synthetic version of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic signal that triggers the pituitary to release LH and FSH, which in turn drive the testes to produce testosterone and sperm. It carries decades-old FDA approval for fertility and diagnostic use, and testosterone-replacement clinics use it — dosed in pulses to mimic the body's natural rhythm — to keep testicular function active alongside exogenous testosterone, similar in purpose to hCG. Head-to-head evidence against hCG, the more established alternative, is mixed, and no study has directly measured its effect on libido itself.

sections.subheader: The Body's Own Upstream Testosterone Trigger
sections.body: Gonadorelin is a synthetic copy of native **GnRH**, the decapeptide the hypothalamus releases in pulses to trigger **LH** and **FSH** secretion from the pituitary — the same upstream signal exogenous testosterone therapy suppresses. By replacing that signal, gonadorelin keeps the testes actively producing their own testosterone and sperm, rather than going dormant.

Exogenous testosterone shuts down the body's own **HPG axis** signaling via negative feedback — the testes stop receiving the LH signal and shrink/reduce function over time. Pulsed gonadorelin dosing alongside TRT is meant to keep that signal alive, preserving testicular size and fertility potential, similar in purpose to **hCG** but acting one step further upstream.

In a 1993 study (Delemarre-van de Waal, n=38) of men with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, pulsatile GnRH administration restored testicular growth and sperm production. Gonadorelin's use for fertility and diagnostic purposes has decades-old **FDA approval**. However, head-to-head trial evidence comparing gonadorelin against **hCG** — the more established TRT-adjunct — for preserving fertility during testosterone therapy is mixed and limited.

Gonadorelin is **prescription-only** and carries older **FDA approval** for fertility and diagnostic use. Its use alongside TRT to preserve testicular function is **off-label** but a legitimate prescribed use through a licensed provider — it is not a controlled substance.

The standard pairing is low-dose, frequent gonadorelin alongside **testosterone cypionate** or other exogenous androgens, specifically to maintain testicular function and fertility potential during TRT — an alternative to hCG for the same purpose.

TRT-adjacent protocols commonly dose gonadorelin at **~100mcg subcutaneous, 2-3 times weekly** — reflecting its short half-life, which favors more frequent, pulsed dosing over the twice-weekly hCG convention. Doses should be individualized by a prescriber based on response.

Reported effects are generally mild — injection-site irritation and occasional headache. Because it stimulates the same axis as exogenous hormone therapy, hormone-sensitive cancers are treated as a contraindication.

Gonadorelin has a plasma **half-life** of roughly 10-40 minutes, consistent with native GnRH's naturally pulsatile secretion pattern — this short half-life is why it's dosed frequently rather than weekly, unlike longer-acting alternatives like hCG.

name: Humanin
subtitle: A mitochondrial-derived peptide discovered protecting neurons from Alzheimer's-linked toxicity — cell and rodent data only, no human trial exists.
description: Humanin is a 24-amino-acid peptide encoded within mitochondrial DNA, first discovered in surviving brain tissue from Alzheimer's patients, where it protected neurons in culture from amyloid-beta toxicity. It's the most-studied member of the mitochondrial-derived peptide family (alongside MOTS-c) and acts as a cytoprotective, anti-inflammatory signal in cell and rodent models. In humans, circulating humanin levels naturally decline with age and correlate with metabolic and mitochondrial health — the basis of longevity interest — but that's observational association, not a measured treatment effect. No trial has ever administered humanin to people.

sections.body: Humanin is unusual among peptides in that it's encoded within **mitochondrial DNA** itself (the 16S rRNA region), not nuclear DNA — placing it, along with **MOTS-c**, in the small 'mitochondrial-derived peptide' family. It acts as a cytoprotective, anti-inflammatory signal, discovered specifically for its ability to rescue neurons from **amyloid-beta** toxicity in cell culture.

sections.subheader: Cytoprotection Across Cell and Rodent Models
sections.body: Beyond its original neuroprotective discovery, humanin has shown cytoprotective effects across various cell and rodent models of stress and injury, consistent with a broader role in cellular stress response tied to mitochondrial signaling — though this breadth of preclinical interest hasn't yet translated to human trial data.

Humanin was first identified by Hashimoto et al. (2001, **PNAS**) in surviving brain tissue from Alzheimer's patients, where it protected neurons from **amyloid-beta** toxicity in vitro. That protective signal has held up across subsequent cell and rodent models of Alzheimer's and stroke — but two decades later, **no human trial** of humanin exists.

sections.subheader: The Longevity Case Is Observational, Not Interventional
sections.body: Separately, human observational data shows circulating humanin levels naturally **decline with age** and correlate with metabolic and mitochondrial health markers — the basis for longevity interest. This is association, not a measured treatment benefit; no study has given humanin to people and measured an outcome.

Humanin is frequently paired with **MOTS-c** in mitochondrial-health/longevity research protocols, since both belong to the same mitochondrial-derived peptide family and are positioned around similar cellular-energy themes. No formal combination trial data exists.

Research-vendor dosing commonly runs **1-2mg subcutaneous daily**. Since no human trial has ever been conducted, this range reflects informal research-community convention only, not clinically validated guidance.

Because no human trial exists, humanin has no characterized human side-effect profile. Active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication given its cytoprotective mechanism, which theoretically could protect damaged cells indiscriminately.
No human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for humanin. All available data comes from cell-culture and rodent models rather than living humans.

name: Sermorelin
subtitle: A classic 29-amino-acid GHRH fragment, historically FDA-approved as Geref — clears fast, keeping GH release in its natural pulsatile rhythm.
description: Sermorelin is a 29-amino-acid fragment of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH 1-29), retaining full biological activity of the native 44-amino-acid hormone. It was FDA-approved as Geref for diagnostic and GH-deficiency use before being discontinued from the market for commercial reasons, though it remains a classic, well-characterized GH secretagogue in research and clinic use. Because it clears the body quickly, it's thought to preserve the pituitary's natural pulsatile GH release pattern better than longer-acting GHRH analogs. Supporting body-composition and sleep data comes mostly from studies of a closely related compound (GHRH 1-29) given intravenously, rather than sermorelin itself administered by injection — an important distinction when weighing the evidence.

sections.subheader: The Minimal Active Fragment of GHRH
sections.body: Sermorelin reproduces the first 29 amino acids of native **growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH)** — the minimal fragment shown to retain full biological activity of the complete 44-amino-acid hormone. It binds the pituitary's **GHRH receptor**, triggering endogenous GH release.

Sermorelin clears the body quickly — its short **half-life** means it produces a single, physiological GH pulse rather than sustained receptor stimulation. This is thought to better preserve the pituitary's natural pulsatile release pattern compared to longer-acting, DAC-modified GHRH analogs like CJC-1295.

sections.subheader: A Real Approval, Discontinued for Business Reasons
sections.body: Sermorelin was **FDA-approved** under the brand **Geref** for diagnostic testing and GH-deficiency treatment before being discontinued from commercial distribution — a business decision, not a safety withdrawal. It remains a well-characterized, classic GH secretagogue.

Much of sermorelin's supporting body-composition and sleep data — including the Khorram 1997 study showing ~1.26kg lean-mass gain in 19 older adults over 16 weeks — actually tested **GHRH(1-29)**, a closely related compound, sometimes by a different route (IV) than the subcutaneous injection people research today. The read-across to injected sermorelin specifically is reasonable given the shared active sequence, but it's indirect, not a direct trial of the product itself.

Sermorelin is commonly paired with **Ipamorelin** — a GHRH analog plus a ghrelin-receptor agonist hitting the GH axis from two distinct receptor angles, the same combined-mechanism logic behind REGEN's existing CJC-1295/Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin blends.

Research-typical dosing is **200–300mcg** subcutaneous once daily, timed before bed to align with the body's natural nighttime GH pulse — mirroring how sermorelin was dosed during its FDA-approved Geref era.

Given its history as an approved drug, sermorelin has a comparatively well-characterized safety profile among GH secretagogues — injection-site flushing, headache, and dizziness are the most commonly reported effects. Active malignancy is a precautionary contraindication given the downstream **IGF-1** stimulation shared across the GH-secretagogue class.

Sermorelin's **half-life** of roughly 10-20 minutes is what produces its brief, physiological-style GH pulse rather than sustained receptor stimulation — the same short-acting design philosophy behind CJC-1295 (no-DAC).

name: SNAP-8
subtitle: The 'topical Botox' marketing peptide — a lab-dish mechanism with no controlled human trial proving the cream actually smooths wrinkles.
description: SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-3) is a topical cosmetic peptide marketed as a 'topical Botox' alternative. The pitch is real biology: in lab dishes, it interferes with the SNARE protein complex that nerve cells use to trigger muscle contraction — the same target Botox hits, just via a different mechanism. What's missing is proof that a topical cream actually penetrates skin deeply enough to reach that target and smooth wrinkles in real people — no controlled human trial of SNAP-8 exists in the medical literature. A related compound, acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline), has more cosmetic-industry studies behind it, but neither comes close to injected Botox's evidence base.

Regulated as a cosmetic ingredient (topical use) — not FDA drug-reviewed for efficacy claims

sections.subheader: A SNARE-Complex Mechanism, Shown in a Dish
sections.body: SNAP-8's proposed mechanism targets the **SNARE complex** — the protein machinery nerve cells use to release neurotransmitter and trigger muscle contraction, the same general target **Botox** (botulinum toxin) hits, though through a completely different biochemical action. This SNARE-interference effect has been demonstrated in **lab-dish (in vitro)** experiments.

The gap between mechanism and marketing claim is **skin penetration** — for SNAP-8 to work as advertised, it needs to cross the skin barrier in meaningful concentration and reach nerve-muscle junctions underneath. No published data confirms this actually happens with topical application at cosmetic concentrations.

No controlled human trial of SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-3) exists in the medical literature. A related compound, **acetyl hexapeptide-8** (marketed as Argireline), has more cosmetic-industry studies behind it, but even that evidence base falls well short of what supports injected Botox.

SNAP-8 is regulated as a **cosmetic ingredient** in topical products — it doesn't require FDA premarket drug approval the way a therapeutic injectable would, but that also means its efficacy claims haven't been through FDA drug-review scrutiny. It's not a controlled substance or a research-chemical-vendor RUO product in its typical topical form.

sections.subheader: Commonly Formulated With Other Peptide Actives
sections.body: SNAP-8 is frequently combined with **GHK-Cu**, **AHK-Cu**, or acetyl hexapeptide-8 in multi-peptide cosmetic serums — a common skincare-industry formulation practice, not a peptide-research stacking protocol with trial support.

As a topical cosmetic ingredient, SNAP-8 doesn't have an injectable dose — usage follows the specific product's formulated concentration and application instructions, typically applied once or twice daily to the target area.

As a topical cosmetic ingredient, SNAP-8 is generally well-tolerated, with rare reports of mild skin irritation or sensitivity in susceptible individuals. There's no systemic exposure concern given its topical-only use and lack of demonstrated significant skin penetration.

sections.subheader: Not Applicable — No Confirmed Systemic Absorption
sections.body: SNAP-8 has no established systemic pharmacokinetic profile since it's used topically and no data confirms meaningful skin penetration, let alone systemic absorption. A conventional plasma **half-life** isn't a meaningful metric for this product category.

name: Dihexa
subtitle: An oral angiotensin IV analog studied as a memory aid in rodents — the foundational animal paper now carries a formal notice of concern, and no human trial exists.
description: Dihexa is a small-molecule angiotensin IV analog studied in rodents as a potential memory-enhancing compound, working through the HGF/c-Met growth-signaling pathway in the brain. The foundational 2013 animal study reported memory restoration in impaired rodents, but no human trial has ever been published, and in 2021 the journal attached a formal notice of concern to that paper. There's also an unresolved safety question: the HGF/c-Met pathway dihexa acts on is one that some cancers also use to grow, and whether that raises tumor risk in people has never been tested.

sections.subheader: An Angiotensin IV Analog Targeting HGF/c-Met
sections.body: Dihexa is a metabolically stabilized analog of **angiotensin IV**, engineered to survive oral administration and activate the **HGF/c-Met** (hepatocyte growth factor / c-Met receptor) signaling pathway in the brain — a pathway involved in synaptogenesis and neuronal growth, distinct from the BDNF/TrkB mechanism used by nootropic peptides like Semax.

Despite its origin as an angiotensin peptide fragment analog, dihexa itself is a **small molecule**, engineered specifically for oral bioavailability and blood-brain barrier penetration — structurally quite different from the injectable peptides in this catalog.

The foundational study (McCoy et al., 2013, **J Pharmacol Exp Ther**) reported that dihexa restored memory in cognitively impaired rodents. This is the primary evidence behind dihexa's reputation as a research nootropic. In **2021**, the journal attached a formal **notice of concern** to this paper — a real, documented red flag on the foundational evidence, not a hypothetical one.

The **HGF/c-Met** pathway dihexa activates is also a pathway some cancers exploit to grow and spread — whether chronic dihexa use raises tumor risk in people has never been studied. Combined with the complete absence of human trial data and the notice of concern on the key animal paper, dihexa carries meaningfully more uncertainty than most compounds in this catalog.

Dihexa has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Given the notice of concern on its foundational study and the untested cancer-pathway question, researchers and users should weigh dihexa's evidence base especially carefully and verify legal status in their jurisdiction before use.

Dihexa is sometimes combined with **Semax** or **Selank** in informal nootropic research stacks, on the logic of pairing HGF/c-Met signaling with BDNF/TrkB pathway activation. No formal combination trial data exists, and neither individual compound's combination safety has been studied.

Research-vendor products are commonly dosed at **5-20mg** orally once daily. Since the foundational evidence is animal-only and the key paper is flagged, this range reflects informal research-community convention rather than any validated human dose-finding data.

Because no human trial has been published, dihexa has no characterized human side-effect profile. Given the untested HGF/c-Met cancer-pathway question, active malignancy and personal/family cancer history are treated as meaningful contraindications here — more seriously than the general precautionary language used for most unapproved compounds in this catalog.
No human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for dihexa. Available PK-adjacent data comes exclusively from the flagged rodent study.

name: Follistatin-344
subtitle: A myostatin-blocking peptide with real biology behind it — but the injectable product sold to researchers has essentially no human evidence of its own.
description: Follistatin-344 is a peptide that binds and neutralizes myostatin, the protein that acts as the body's natural brake on muscle growth — blocking myostatin is the same biological logic behind naturally myostatin-deficient animals (and rare human cases) developing dramatically increased muscle mass. The biology is real, but the human evidence gap is unusually wide: the only human data supporting follistatin's muscle effects comes from a one-time gene-therapy trial in Becker muscular dystrophy patients — a virus delivering the follistatin gene directly into muscle — which is a completely different intervention from the injectable peptide sold by research vendors. That injectable product has no published human studies of its own at any dose.

sections.subheader: Blocking the Body's Brake on Muscle Growth
sections.body: Follistatin-344 binds and neutralizes **myostatin**, a protein that normally restrains skeletal muscle growth by signaling through the activin receptor pathway. Animals and rare humans with naturally low myostatin activity show dramatically increased muscle mass — this real biology is the entire rationale behind follistatin as a muscle-growth research compound.

sections.subheader: A Real Peptide, Unlike Steroidal Myostatin-Adjacent Compounds
sections.body: Unlike steroidal compounds that claim myostatin-pathway effects as a side mechanism (e.g. YK-11), follistatin-344 acts directly and specifically on myostatin itself as its primary, dedicated mechanism — the most mechanistically 'clean' myostatin-inhibition approach among peptides sold in this space.

sections.subheader: The Human Data Is From a Different Intervention Entirely
sections.body: The only human evidence connecting follistatin to muscle improvement comes from Mendell et al. (2015, **Molecular Therapy**), a **gene-therapy** trial in 6 Becker muscular dystrophy patients — a virus delivering the follistatin *gene* directly into muscle tissue, a one-time genetic intervention. 4 of 6 patients walked farther on a 6-minute walk test. This is fundamentally different from injecting the follistatin *peptide* itself, which is what research vendors actually sell.

Follistatin-344 has no FDA-approved indication and is **not approved for human consumption**. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO), and — importantly — the injectable peptide product itself has **no published human studies at any dose**. This is one of the largest gaps between marketing claims and actual product-specific evidence among compounds in this catalog. Researchers and users should verify the legal status of follistatin-344 in their jurisdiction and weigh this evidence gap carefully.

Follistatin-344 is sometimes combined with GH secretagogue blends like **CJC-1295 (no-DAC) + Ipamorelin** in research protocols targeting muscle growth through two separate pathways — myostatin inhibition plus GH/IGF-1 stimulation. No formal combination trial data exists.

Research-vendor products are commonly dosed at **100-300mcg** subcutaneous once daily. Since the injectable peptide has no published human dose-finding study at all, this range reflects informal research-community convention only.

sections.subheader: No Human Safety Data for the Injectable Peptide
sections.body: Because the injectable peptide has never been studied in humans, there is no characterized human side-effect profile for this specific product. The gene-therapy trial (a different intervention) reported generally mild tolerability, but this doesn't transfer to the injectable peptide's safety profile. Active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication given myostatin's broader role in cell growth regulation.

sections.subheader: Not Established for the Injectable Peptide
sections.body: No human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for the injectable follistatin-344 peptide. The gene-therapy trial doesn't produce comparable PK data since it's a fundamentally different delivery mechanism (viral gene expression vs. direct peptide injection).

name: hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)
subtitle: An FDA-approved hormone that mimics LH, restoring the body's own testosterone and sperm production — the label dates to 1962.
description: hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) is a hormone that mimics LH (luteinizing hormone), the pituitary's own signal telling the testes to produce testosterone. By standing in for that signal, hCG raises a man's endogenous testosterone and keeps sperm production going — restoring the hormonal machinery that testosterone therapy would otherwise suppress. It carries a genuine FDA label dating back to 1962, approved for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and fertility use, and is one of the most established TRT-adjunct compounds in clinical use. It is not the same as the 'hCG diet' — that use isn't part of its approved label or supporting evidence.

sections.subheader: Mimicking LH to Restart Testicular Function
sections.body: hCG is structurally similar enough to **LH** (luteinizing hormone) that it binds and activates the same **LH receptor** on testicular Leydig cells, which respond by producing **testosterone** — the same signal the pituitary would normally send. This is why hCG can restore the body's own testosterone production even when the pituitary itself isn't sending that signal, whether due to a medical condition or exogenous testosterone therapy's suppressive feedback.

Because it directly stimulates the testes rather than relying on upstream pituitary signaling, hCG keeps **spermatogenesis** active during testosterone replacement therapy — a key reason it's the most established TRT-adjunct compound for men who want to preserve fertility while on exogenous testosterone.

hCG's **FDA approval** for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and fertility use dates back to **1962** — one of the oldest, most established hormone therapies in this catalog. In a 2019 study (Madhusoodanan et al., n=20) of men taking hCG as monotherapy, testosterone rose approximately **50%**, with roughly half reporting symptom improvement — low libido and erectile dysfunction were each the presenting complaint in 45% of participants.

hCG is **prescription-only** and **FDA-approved**, with an exceptionally long track record. It should be obtained through a licensed prescriber and pharmacy. Note: the popular 'hCG diet' (very-low-calorie dieting combined with hCG for weight loss) is **not** part of hCG's approved label or supported by its evidence base — the FDA has specifically warned against marketing hCG for weight loss.

The standard, well-established pairing is hCG alongside **testosterone cypionate** or other exogenous androgens, specifically to preserve testicular size and fertility during TRT — the most clinically mainstream TRT-adjunct pairing in this catalog, alongside **gonadorelin** as an alternative.

TRT-adjacent protocols commonly dose hCG at **250–500 IU subcutaneous, 2-3 times weekly** — lower and more frequent than the larger doses used for fertility-induction protocols, which are prescriber-directed and higher.

Because raising testosterone via hCG also increases **aromatization** to estradiol, higher doses can cause estrogen-related effects (water retention, gynecomastia sensitivity) — sometimes managed with an aromatase inhibitor like **anastrozole**. Injection-site irritation and mood changes are also reported. Hormone-sensitive cancers and precocious puberty are contraindications.
hCG has a plasma **half-life** of roughly 24-36 hours, notably longer than most peptide hormones in this catalog — which is why it's dosed just 2-3 times weekly rather than daily.

name: SLU-PP-332
subtitle: A pan-ERR agonist nicknamed the 'exercise pill' — reduced fat mass and raised fatty-acid oxidation in obese mice, with zero human trials as of 2026.
description: SLU-PP-332 is a small-molecule pan-ERR (estrogen-related receptor) agonist that reproduces some of the metabolic gene-expression changes seen with endurance exercise — increasing fatty-acid oxidation, mitochondrial content, and energy expenditure. In diet-induced-obese mice, it reduced body weight (roughly 12%) and fat-mass accumulation without reducing food intake, suggesting a metabolic rather than appetite-suppressing effect, distinct from the GLP-1 class. As of 2026 it has never been studied in humans — all supporting data comes from mouse and cell experiments.

sections.body: SLU-PP-332 activates all three **ERR** (estrogen-related receptor) subtypes — nuclear receptors that sit downstream of **PGC-1α**, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis normally activated by endurance exercise. Pharmacologically activating ERR reproduces part of that gene-expression program — increased **fatty-acid oxidation**, mitochondrial content, and oxidative muscle fiber type — without requiring the exercise itself, earning it the informal nickname 'exercise in a pill.'

Unlike **GLP-1** class drugs, SLU-PP-332's weight effects in mice occurred **without reduced food intake** — the mechanism is about increasing energy expenditure and fat oxidation, not suppressing appetite. This makes it mechanistically distinct from the semaglutide/tirzepatide family despite both being studied for weight-related outcomes.

Billon et al. (2024, **J Pharmacol Exp Ther**) found SLU-PP-332 reduced body weight (~12%) and fat-mass accumulation in diet-induced-obese mice without reducing food intake. A companion 2023 study (**ACS Chem Biol**) found it increased oxidative type IIa muscle fibers and mitochondrial content — consistent with a genuine endurance-training-like metabolic shift, at least in mice.

SLU-PP-332 is **not FDA-approved** and has never been studied in humans as of 2026 — every claim rests on mouse and cell data. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of SLU-PP-332 in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use, and should weigh the complete absence of human data accordingly.

SLU-PP-332 is sometimes discussed alongside its orally-active successor compound **SLU-PP-915** in research contexts, though they're typically used as alternatives (injectable vs. oral) rather than combined — both target the same ERR pathway.

Research-vendor products are commonly dosed at **25-50mg** subcutaneous once daily. Since no human trial exists, this range reflects informal research-community convention extrapolated from mouse dosing, not validated human guidance.

Because no human trial has been published, there is no characterized human side-effect profile for SLU-PP-332. Active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication given the broad nuclear-receptor mechanism affecting cellular metabolism genome-wide.

No human pharmacokinetic study — absorption, **half-life**, clearance — has been published for SLU-PP-332. Notably, the original compound required injection to show effects in mice, which is part of what motivated development of the orally-active follow-on compound, SLU-PP-915.

name: SLU-PP-915
subtitle: The first orally-active pan-ERR agonist — raised exercise capacity in mice even when dosed orally, where its predecessor SLU-PP-332 needed injection.
description: SLU-PP-915 is a follow-on compound to SLU-PP-332, engineered specifically to retain pan-ERR agonist activity when dosed orally — its predecessor lost effect unless injected. In mice, it increased treadmill exercise capacity in a dose-dependent way, with the effect holding up when given orally, and separately upregulated the same mitochondrial/exercise-response gene program (PGC-1alpha, Ddit4, Pdk4) as SLU-PP-332. Like its predecessor, all supporting data is from mice — no human trial has been published.

sections.subheader: The Same ERR Mechanism, Now Oral
sections.body: SLU-PP-915 activates the same **pan-ERR** (estrogen-related receptor) pathway as its predecessor SLU-PP-332, driving the **PGC-1α**-linked mitochondrial biogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation gene program associated with endurance exercise. Its defining engineering achievement is retaining this activity when dosed **orally** — SLU-PP-332 required injection to show effects in mice.

sections.subheader: Exercise Capacity, Not Just Metabolic Markers
sections.body: SLU-PP-915's headline mouse result is functional, not just biochemical: increased **treadmill exercise capacity**, in a dose-dependent way, that held up when the compound was given orally — a more direct performance readout than the fat-mass/gene-expression endpoints emphasized in SLU-PP-332's data.

sections.subheader: First Oral Compound in This Class to Work
sections.body: Billon et al. (2025, **J Pharmacol Exp Ther**) reported dose-dependent exercise-capacity gains in mice that were retained when the compound was dosed orally (adjusted for exposure) — the first orally active compound in the SLU-PP series to show this. An earlier 2023 discovery paper (Xu et al., **Eur J Med Chem**) found a single injected dose raised exercise-response genes, and a 6-day course enhanced endurance.

SLU-PP-915 is **not FDA-approved** and has never been studied in humans as of 2026 — like its predecessor, every claim rests on mouse data. It is sold exclusively as a research-grade compound (RUO). Researchers and users should verify the legal status of SLU-PP-915 in their jurisdiction prior to purchase or use.
SLU-PP-915 is generally used as an **oral alternative** to injectable SLU-PP-332 rather than combined with it — both target the same ERR pathway, so stacking them wouldn't add a distinct mechanism.

Research-vendor products are commonly dosed at **10-25mg** orally once daily. Since no human trial exists, this range reflects informal research-community convention extrapolated from mouse dosing, not validated human guidance.

Because no human trial has been published, there is no characterized human side-effect profile for SLU-PP-915. Active malignancy is treated as a precautionary contraindication given the broad nuclear-receptor mechanism affecting cellular metabolism genome-wide.

sections.subheader: First Orally Bioavailable Compound in Its Class
sections.body: No formal human pharmacokinetic study exists, but SLU-PP-915's defining property — relative to SLU-PP-332 — is retaining meaningful exposure and effect when dosed **orally** in mice, the property its structural optimization specifically targeted.
